# Training-set composition steers and locks in the Fourier features of grokking transformers

*Authors: to be decided by the user (see paper/STATUS, 'Offen für den Nutzer').*

*Generated by `lab/paper/build_manuscript.py` from `draft_short.md`; do not edit by hand.*

## Abstract

Networks that grok modular arithmetic use a sparse set of Fourier features, and which frequencies a network uses is usually treated as an outcome of its initialization. We show that the composition of the training set steers this choice. In pre-registered replications on fresh seeds, engineered training splits enrich five prescribed frequencies in the embedding of a one-layer transformer for addition mod 113 and 97, multiplication mod 113 and the dihedral group D59 (50 seeds per task), and equal-norm embedding perturbations along the steered frequencies reduce the logit margin more than along controls (20 seeds per task; D59 after grokking). In addition mod 113, even an ordinary uniform 30 % split biases the learned frequencies, though far from determining them, and engineered splits generalize in about 6.5× fewer steps than uniform random splits and 7.5× fewer than a control with the same number of pairs per output (geometric means, times bounded at 8000 steps; 20/20 units). The choice starts to persist within 25 to 50 full-batch steps (addition mod 113, learning rate 10⁻³): the sign of an ablation contrast between old and new target frequencies reverses between a data switch after 25 and after 50 steps (it tracks embedding energy), and a switch after 25 steps delays grokking by about ×1.8, whereas a switch to new pairs with the same targets did not delay it on average. All of these results use full-batch training. Under i.i.d. minibatches (batch 256 and 64) the steering was confirmed on fresh seeds; a fixed data order did not shift the steered frequencies at 30 % data, so no conflict could be tested (pilot); at batch 256 the choice persists from a half-point of 114 steps (10 fresh seeds, energy measure), later than in full batch (pilot). We report effect sizes with confidence intervals, the limits of each measure (functional sensitivity follows spectral energy), and negative results.

## 1 Introduction

Small networks trained on modular arithmetic first memorize their training pairs and only much later generalize ("grokking"; Power et al. 2022). The generalizing solution computes with a handful of Fourier frequencies of the group (Nanda et al. 2023), or with a few irreducible representations for other finite groups (Chughtai et al. 2023). *Which* frequencies a particular network uses has been described as arbitrary across runs (Chughtai et al. 2023); many frequency sets implement the task equally well (Gromov 2023), and at a fixed training set, hyperparameters and initialization can even change the type of algorithm (Zhong et al. 2023). Recent theory attributes the competition between frequencies to the initialization (He et al. 2026a). For uniform data it derives the order of learned representations from the Fourier statistics of the input encoding (Marchetti et al. 2026). With one-hot tokens that encoding favours no frequency in cyclic groups and ties irreducible representations of equal dimension, and the role of the train–test split has been named as open (He et al. 2026b).

We ask whether the training set itself can decide this choice. In the one-layer transformer of a previous grokking study, with fixed one-hot tokens and full-batch AdamW, we construct training splits whose pair mask concentrates its spectrum on five prescribed frequencies. This lever differs from three known ones. LeDoux (2026) showed that a fixed, structured order of examples sets the fundamental frequency under minibatch training, with the same frequency across random training subsets. Marchetti et al. (2026) work through encoding statistics. In recursive feature machines, training sets that are invariant under a subgroup of the task's symmetry group prevent generalization, and the learned feature matrix then encodes only that subgroup (Tomàs Bernal et al. 2026; kernels only, symmetric splits, no prescribed frequencies). Here only *which* pairs are shown changes, the split has no built-in symmetry, and the targets are prescribed frequencies. Salah and Yevick (2024) restricted the training set of modular addition by removing symmetry-related pairs, but measured only whether the network generalized, not which frequencies it learned. In language models and related architectures, data, architecture, optimizer and tokenizer decide whether periodic number features become geometrically separable (Fu et al. 2026). For word embeddings, co-occurrence symmetry explains circular and other low-dimensional structures in theory, matched empirically in language models (Karkada et al. 2026). Our setting isolates the data lever in a task where the learned algorithm is known. A first-order argument accounts for the initial enrichment: the Fourier power of the first embedding gradient follows the coherent spectrum of the training-pair mask (post hoc, Appendix G). It does not predict what we measure beyond that: the enrichment survives grokking, comes with a functional sensitivity, speeds up generalization, and becomes persistent within tens of steps.

We report three main pre-registered results, and a minibatch extension (Section 6), with fresh seeds and frozen analysis manifests. (1) Engineered splits steer the learned frequencies in four tasks, including a non-abelian group, and networks are more sensitive along the steered frequencies; an ordinary random split also biases the choice, though far from determining it (Section 3; sensitivity follows spectral energy). (2) Engineered splits generalize several times faster than uniform random splits and than a control with the same number of pairs per output (Section 4). (3) The choice starts to persist within 25 to 50 full-batch steps (at learning rate 10⁻³). A switch after 25 steps delays grokking by about ×1.8, one after 50 steps does not, and a switch to new pairs with the same target frequencies costs no time on average (Section 5). That early training can resist later data is familiar from critical learning periods (Achille et al. 2019), the primacy bias (Nikishin et al. 2022) and warm starting (Ash and Adams 2020). In fine-tuning, fixed-clock optimizer memory makes data-order effects first order in the learning rate (Sweeney 2026). What we add is a measured time scale of tens of steps for a prescribed feature choice under a controlled data switch.

Because LeDoux's order effect arises under minibatch training, Section 6 (L0) tests whether the steering survives minibatch training and a structured example order that favours other frequencies. All claims hold for one model family and for constructed splits; R4, R5 and Section 5 hold for addition mod 113 only, except the persistence window in embedding energy (also addition mod 97 and multiplication mod 113, R11). Explorations, resets, the optimizer clock of the lock-in, and a first-order account are in the appendix. Novelty statements mean "not found in our search", not "new".

## 2 Setup

**Model and training.** One-layer transformer of the original GROKVERSE study (following Nanda et al. 2023, without biases): embedding W_E and positional embedding (d_model = 128), one attention layer with four heads of width 32, a ReLU MLP of width 512, no layer normalization, untied readout. Inputs are (a, b, =); the loss is the cross-entropy at the last position. Training is full-batch AdamW (learning rate 10⁻³, weight decay 1, β = (0.9, 0.98)) on 30 % of all pairs. The two arms of a seed share the initialization; only the training set differs. Confirmation blocks ran on one GPU after a statistical equivalence check against the CPU path; runs compared within a block used the same device.

**Tasks.** Addition mod 113 (primary) and 97, multiplication mod 113 (frequencies in the discrete-logarithm coordinate, Z_112; pairs with a zero operand are not in the group and keep uniform weight in the split construction), and composition in the dihedral group D59 (order 118; the 29 two-dimensional irreducible representations).

**Engineered splits.** Per seed, two disjoint target sets of five frequencies each. Arm F draws 30 % of all pairs without replacement with weights q(a, b) = max(0.05, 1 + ε·w(a, b)), w(a, b) = (1/5) Σ_{k∈T_F} cos(2πk·u(a)/n + φ_k(c)) with the group coordinate u(a), the output c and a random phase per target and output (for D59 an irrep trace); arm G likewise; ε = 2. Token counts are no more unequal than in a random split (coefficient of variation 0.14 in the pilot construction), although their spectrum is also target-enriched (Appendix G). The main difference lies in the spectrum of the pair mask (centred target share 0.194 against 0.089 for a random split).

**Switch protocol (Result 3; addition mod 113).** A common held-out test set (20 %) is removed first; two pair-disjoint training sets A and B of 3831 pairs pick their pairs in alternation from their own weighted orders (steering strength calibrated to a mask target share of 0.185). A run trains t steps on A, switches to B (optimizer state kept) and trains a fixed further budget; each seed runs both directions.

**Measures.** On the group-element rows X of W_E, P_k(X) is the power in the Fourier (irrep) subspace of k. *Steering*: Δ_pow = log[P_F(T_F)/P_F(T_G)] + log[P_G(T_G)/P_G(T_F)] at step 2000. *Margin sensitivity*: the drop of the mean correct-class logit margin on pairs outside both splits after a step X − δ·u_S, δ = 0.02‖X‖, along the arm's own target set S (u_S = P_S X/‖P_S X‖, the normalized projection of X onto the frequency (irrep) subspaces of S), minus the mean drop along four control sets (drawn without both target sets and the harmonics 2k), averaged over both arms. *Persistence*: π = (L_switch − L_pureB)/(L_pureA − L_pureB), L = log[P(T_A)/P(T_B)] of the final embedding, averaged over both switch directions (an unbounded affine index, not a probability). *Ablation contrast*: accuracy after removing the new target subspaces from W_E minus accuracy after removing the old ones. *Time to generalization*: first evaluation with test accuracy ≥ 0.95, evaluated every 25 steps and bounded at a fixed horizon: in R5 a stable event (≥ 0.95 at s, s + 25 and s + 50 after train accuracy ≥ 0.99), bounded at 8000 steps; in R6/R8 the first crossing counted from step 0, bounded at 2000, compared as log2 ratios with the destination-only run.

**Protocol.** Every confirmation block was registered before its runs: hypotheses, primary measure, minimum effect, family with Holm correction, sample size, a reserved block of fresh seeds, and the previously seen data with the decisions they influenced. A committed manifest stores code hashes, and the analysis accepts only runs bound to it (Appendix H); the frozen version of a registration is the one at its manifest commit (some file names still carry the suffix DRAFT from drafting). Holm correction applies within each block's family; no correction is applied across the blocks of Table 1. Intervals are percentile bootstrap intervals over seeds. Pilots are reported separately as explorations. Blocks are named by short identifiers (P1, R4, …); Table 1 maps each identifier to its hypothesis, manifest commit, fresh seeds and number of runs (generated from the frozen manifests, `figures/table_registrations.py`).

## 3 Result 1: the composition of the training set steers the learned frequencies

**Steering (P1, pre-registered replication on 50 fresh seeds per task; tasks chosen as steerable in pilots).** For each seed we built two engineered splits F and G of the same size whose pair masks concentrate their spectrum on five disjoint target frequencies (irreducible representations for D59), and trained the same initialization on each. Only the split differs, so the comparison is a paired intervention. At step 2000 the relative W_E energy of the own against the other targets, Δ_pow, was 8.24 [7.92, 8.54] for addition mod 113, 8.09 [7.75, 8.43] for multiplication mod 113, 6.11 [5.79, 6.43] for addition mod 97 and 2.64 [2.55, 2.73] for D59, positive in 50/50 seeds in every task (Holm-p ≤ 1.5·10⁻⁵, worst case and at the resolution of 200 000 random sign flips; Figure 1). Descriptively, the five own targets carried on average 0.80 of the embedding's group power in addition mod 113 (chance 0.089), 0.79 in multiplication mod 113, 0.69 in addition mod 97 and 0.44 in D59 (chance 0.17). For D59, step 2000 is before grokking; after grokking (P2f, 12 000 steps) the own irreducible representations carried a median 0.98 of the energy. In the other three tasks the steering is not a pre-grokking transient: in separate stored runs (P2d/P2e, 20 other seeds per task; post hoc exploration, not P1) Δ_pow stayed positive in every seed at every stored step and grew after generalization (numbers in Appendix K). The steering also held when one hyperparameter deviated (R1; weakest where few runs had generalized by step 2000), in a shared-embedding MLP (at 10 000 steps, after grokking), at 4× width, in a two-layer transformer (smaller: −2.70 [−3.16, −2.18] against one layer; R7), and for non-modular integer addition, where no network generalized, so there it is a property of the representation only (P4). Details in Appendix A.

**Functional sensitivity (P2d, P2e, P2f).** A step of norm 0.02·‖X‖ (X = number rows of W_E) along the steered frequencies reduced the mean correct-class logit margin on pairs outside both splits more than steps along four pre-specified control sets: 0.250 [0.229, 0.270] (addition mod 113, 4000 steps), 0.291 [0.268, 0.308] (multiplication mod 113, 8000 steps), 0.294 [0.275, 0.312] (addition mod 97, 8000 steps), each 20/20 seeds, and D = 0.233 [0.214, 0.253] for D59 after grokking (12 000 steps, 20/20). In the addition-mod-113 switch models where we tested it (not the P2d–P2f models), this sensitivity followed the energy distribution: at equal removed energy the dominant set had no advantage. We therefore claim sensitivity, not use beyond energy. Three earlier registered functional variants were not evaluable, aborted or not confirmed; they are reported in Appendix B.

**An ordinary random split also shapes the choice (R4, addition mod 113, 60 fresh units).** Each unit crossed two initializations with two uniform 30 % splits (8000 steps). Networks sharing a split had more similar embedding spectra than networks sharing nothing: after 8000 steps, Δ_split = 0.118 [0.079, 0.157] in an energy-weighted cosine (48/60 units positive, 42/60 above the minimum effect), and before grokking the rank order of all 56 frequencies was also more alike (Spearman at step 2000, 0.33 [0.30, 0.36]). Descriptively the shared split raised similarity more than a shared initialization, but it is far from determining the choice: networks with the same split share on average about one of their five strongest frequencies, against about one half without a shared split (chance 25/56 ≈ 0.45). This concerns representation energy, not use (no ablation), in one task and one architecture. The engineered splits of Result 1 are thus consistent with a stronger dose of an effect that already acts on ordinary random splits.

**What this shows and what it does not.** In a paired design with engineered splits, the choice of training pairs enriches the prescribed frequencies in four tasks, with fixed one-hot tokens and full-batch training. Section 6 (L0) tests whether the steering survives minibatch training and a competing order signal. LeDoux (2026) reports the same frequency across random training subsets under a structured example order at p = 9973, plausibly a different regime (not measured) with ≈ 80× more pairs, in which the spectral fluctuations of a uniform random subset, shrinking roughly as 1/√n, are about 9× smaller.

## 4 Result 2: engineered splits generalize earlier (R5)

**Design (pre-registered, 20 fresh units, addition mod 113, 8000 steps).** Per unit, seven training sets of 3831 pairs share one held-out test set and one initialization: a uniform random split R, engineered splits with ε = 2 for two target sets and ε = 1 and 8 for one of them, and for each ε = 2 split a control D with exactly the same number of training pairs per output value (per anti-diagonal), but with positions drawn uniformly within each anti-diagonal. The event is a stable rise of test accuracy to ≥ 0.95 after train accuracy ≥ 0.99; times are bounded at 8000 steps.

**Result.** The engineered split generalized in ×6.5 [5.3, 7.9] fewer steps than the random split (target set A) and ×7.5 [6.5, 8.6] fewer than the matched control (mean over both target sets; geometric means of bounded time ratios; 20/20 units in the same direction for both; Holm-p ≤ 2·10⁻⁵, at the resolution of 100 000 permutations; Figure 2). Higher ε was faster (ε = 1 took ×14.4 [12.4, 16.6] as long as ε = 8; secondary, outside the family; ε changes pair selection and truncation together, so this is not by itself evidence for concentration). Median bounded times were 775–813 steps (ε = 2), 6163 (R) and 6850–7513 (D). By step 8000, 16/20 random-split units and 14/20 and 11/20 control units had generalized; the others count at the bound, so the ratios are conservative.

**What this shows and what it does not.** At matched per-output counts, the arrangement of the pairs within the anti-diagonals accounts for the speed-up relative to D (this arrangement carries both the concentrated mask spectrum and a target-enriched spectrum of the token counts, which D does not separate); the output marginals alone do not produce it. D matches only the frozen statistics, so finer geometric differences are not excluded. "Earlier" means an earlier stable rise within 8000 steps, not a higher final accuracy. Known levers on the grokking delay include the initialization scale and weight norm (Kumar et al. 2024; Liu et al. 2023; Khanh et al. 2026), and that early task-aligned embedding structure shortens it is known from other interventions (Howe 2026b; GrokTransfer); and that the makeup rather than the size of the training data governs how fast grokking proceeds was reported for implicit reasoning, where speed tracks the ratio of inferred to atomic facts (Wang et al. 2024; there, changing the ratio also changes the training size). The contribution here is that the choice of training pairs alone shortens the delay, at matched size, initialization and test set. Limits: one task, one architecture and optimizer setting (lr 10⁻³, weight decay 1), train fraction 30 %, ε = 2 for the primary contrasts.

## 5 Result 3: the choice starts to persist within 25–50 full-batch steps (P3, N29, R6, R8; addition mod 113)

**Persistence after a switch (P3, N28; pre-registered, 30 fresh seeds each).** After 25 steps on a first engineered split and 2000 steps on a pair-disjoint second split, final models sat at π = 0.351 of the normalized log-energy distance between the two pure endpoints (persistence π); the excess over the best tested static additive trace was 0.293 [0.263, 0.322] (30/30), where a trace is the π of the pure-destination embedding plus c times the embedding change of the first 25 steps, maximized over c ∈ [0, 1]. Zeroing Adam's first moment at the switch lowered π (separate block N28, 0.340 → 0.189), and ten extra pre-switch steps compensated this, compatible with a reading in which longer exposure to the source split builds the persistence (Appendix K); that the first moment carries such a signal is known from other settings (Sweeney 2026; Xu 2026).

**An ablation contrast reverses (N29, 20 fresh seeds).** Removing all five target frequencies from W_E after a switch and 4000 further steps: after a switch at step 50, removing the old targets cost 0.903 [0.846, 0.953] more test accuracy than removing the new ones (20/20 seeds above 0.3); after a switch at step 25, removing the new targets cost 0.603 [0.498, 0.700] more (17/20). The embedding energy points the same way (post hoc), so the contrast does not separate reliance from energy. The two time points bracket a reversal; a network-wide or irreversible commitment is not shown.

**A switch inside this window costs time (R6, 30 fresh seeds).** With b the first step with test accuracy ≥ 0.95 (bounded at 2000) and C(t) the log2 time ratio against training on the destination split only, a switch at step 25 delayed grokking by C(25) = +0.85 [0.73, 0.96] (a factor ≈ 1.8; 29/30 seeds; Figure 3) and more than a switch at step 50 (C(25) − C(50) = +1.25 [0.97, 1.50]; 28/30). Across the grid (t = 10, 20, 25, 30, 40, 50, 75), the mean cost was positive at t = 10–40 (at 40 only +0.27, 22/30) and negative at 50 and 75 (switched runs then generalized earlier on average, 24/30 seeds at 50 and 30/30 at 75, so C(t) is a net effect of interference and of progress made on the engineered source split). C(t) compares regimes: t destination updates are replaced by source updates, no mixed A∪B control was run, and time to threshold is evaluated every 25 steps. Switch runs that had not generalized by step 2000 count at the bound (all destination-only runs had), so C(t) underestimates the delay where it is largest (counts in Appendix K). The confirmed difference between 25 and 50 argues against a reading in which the cost only reflects fewer updates on the destination split, which predicts C(50) ≥ C(25).

**A change of targets costs far more than a change of pairs (R8, 25 fresh seeds).** A switch at step 25 to a pair-disjoint split with the same five targets and matched steering strength did not delay grokking on average (−0.15 log2; 8/25 seeds slower), whereas the switch to other targets did (+0.66; 24/25); difference +0.81 [0.57, 1.04]. The delay is therefore not a generic cost of an early change of training pairs, nor of fewer destination updates alone. Because the same-target split has partly reversed wave phases, a pure phase conflict is not excluded. Several switch runs had not generalized by step 2000 (A→B 20/25, B→A 15/25 did; same-target switches 24/25 each), so C_AB is bounded. One task, one architecture.

**The window generalizes beyond addition mod 113 (R11, the same 30 fresh seeds for both tasks).** With a one-direction switch at 25 or 50 steps, the first split's choice persisted mostly after 50 but not after 25 steps also in addition mod 97 (π(25) = 0.38, π(50) = 0.90; difference +0.52 [0.45, 0.59], 30/30 seeds) and in multiplication mod 113 (0.27 and 0.74; +0.47 [0.40, 0.54], 30/30); all six registered tests held (Holm). This is the embedding-energy measure only; the ablation contrast and the time cost were not re-tested there (details in Appendix K).

## 6 L0: set composition against data order under minibatch training

**Question.** All results above use full-batch training. LeDoux (2026) found, under minibatch training with a fixed, structured example order, the same fundamental frequency across random training subsets. We ask (i) whether the steering by the set survives i.i.d. minibatch training, (ii) what happens when a fixed order favours other frequencies than the set, and (iii) when the choice starts to persist under minibatches.

**Design.** Addition mod 113, the setup of Section 2, AdamW with i.i.d. minibatches of 256 or 64 pairs (a pilot with 8 seeds, also ran full batch with a matched 30 000-step budget and SGD with momentum). The conflict arm uses a fixed stride order after LeDoux (pairs sorted by (a mod 10, a), identical in every epoch), whose spectral weight lies on O = {11, 12, 22, 23, 34, 45}; the engineered targets exclude O. Because a first-order computation made before any run (Appendix I) predicted that the order can compete with the set within the full-batch lock-in window only for long epochs, an arm with batch 16 (240 steps per epoch; weight decay 0.1, because weight decay 1 did not generalize there in 30 000 steps, a regime change) was added before any run. LeDoux's order effect was strong at 0.3 % data (≈ 1165 steps per epoch); our regime is far from it. Readings were fixed before the runs; the conflict is judged only if the order acts at all.

**Steering survives minibatch training (confirmed).** On 10 fresh seeds (L0, frozen before any run), Δ_pow was 9.43 [9.06, 9.81] at batch 256 and 9.60 [8.79, 10.46] at batch 64 (10/10 seeds each; Holm-p 4·10⁻¹² and 3·10⁻⁹; Figure 4a). In the pilot, the same batch sizes gave 9.60 and 9.85 against 10.28 for full batch with the same budget. At batch 64, 12 of 20 confirmation runs had not settled at the end of the budget (final train accuracy below 0.99), so the claim is steering at the end of the budget, not in converged networks. The steering also held at batch 16 with weight decay 0.1 (pilot, 8 seeds: 9.21 [8.82, 9.60]; Appendix I).

**Order against set (pilots, exploration).** At batch 256 and 64 the stride order did not shift the learned frequencies (peak frequency in O in 0/16 runs each), so by the pre-set rule the conflict was not testable there, nor at batch 16 (order-alone reading 'unclear'). Descriptively, the order raised the order share on random splits (+0.16 [0.07, 0.24]) but not on the engineered splits, where it only delayed generalization (≈ ×1.6, 15/16 pairs). This is consistent with LeDoux's remark that the importance of order scales inversely with the content signal of the data. SGD with momentum could not be calibrated and is not evaluable.

**The lock-in window under minibatches (N54b confirmed; full-batch comparison from pilots).** In pilots, a switch after 25 or 50 steps at batch 256 left no persistent trace (8 seeds; π ≈ 0, against π(50) = 0.87 in full batch on the same seeds), and the window lay later in steps but earlier in epochs (pilots: half-point ≈ 133 steps = 8.9 epochs at batch 256, against ≈ 31 steps = 31 epochs in full batch; energy measure). On 10 fresh seeds (N54b, frozen before any run, 840 runs) the half-point t½ at lr 10⁻³ was 58, 114 and 289 steps at batch 1024, 256 and 64; it grew with the steps per epoch N/B (Figure 4b, c) with a mean log–log slope α = 0.583 [0.560, 0.606] (registered square-root band [0.3, 0.7]; Holm-p 5·10⁻⁶). Doubling the learning rate raised the slope in every seed (Δα = +0.139 [0.098, 0.178], 10/10, Holm-p 6·10⁻⁵): it shortened lock-in to 0.58 [0.54, 0.62] of its duration at batch 1024 but only to 0.85 [0.78, 0.92] at batch 64. log t½ is curved (two-point slopes 0.48 and 0.68 at lr 10⁻³), so α is an average slope over N/B = 3.7–60, not a clean power law; with N fixed, steps per epoch and batch size are not separated. In our search (29 September 2026) we did not find a prior measurement of a square-root batch-size scaling of an early lock-in time at fixed learning rate. The pilots, a model comparison fixed before the N54b results and all limits are in Appendix I.

## 7 Discussion and limitations

**What the three results say together.** In small networks trained full-batch on these tasks, which pairs are shown steers which frequencies the embedding favours, strongly for engineered splits and weakly for random ones (Result 1; measured as embedding energy). In addition mod 113 and one architecture, engineered splits also generalize several times faster at fixed size (Result 2). In the same setting, full-batch and at the default learning rate and weight decay, the choice starts to persist within 25 to 50 steps, as measured by embedding energy and by an ablation contrast that does not separate reliance from energy (Result 3). None of this requires changing the tokens, the architecture or the loss.

**Limitations.** (i) *Regime:* unless stated otherwise, results use full-batch AdamW (lr 10⁻³, weight decay 1, β = 0.9/0.98) and a train fraction of 30 %. R1 varies one hyperparameter at a time for the steering. The reversal of Result 3 held at double learning rate (switch at 12 against 50 steps) but its switching side was not confirmed at 0.3× weight decay (Appendix A, R2). Minibatch training and data order are tested only in L0 (Section 6); the 25–50-step figure of Result 3 is a full-batch result. (ii) *Scope:* steering holds in four tasks; other architectures (MLP, 4× width, two layers) and functional sensitivity were each tested in fewer settings (Appendices A, B and E). R4, R5 and Result 3 hold for addition mod 113 in one architecture only, except that the persistence window of Result 3 (energy measure) was also confirmed for addition mod 97 and multiplication mod 113 (R11). Steering also held in one small language-model configuration (LM1, Appendix J). (iii) *Measures:* functional sensitivity follows spectral energy in the addition-mod-113 switch models where this was tested (not in the P2d–P2f models). We make no claim about use beyond energy. Resets (Appendix C) localize sensitivity, not mechanism. (iv) *Time scales* are counted in optimizer steps. Which clock governs the persistence is only partly settled: it is not the step count alone (R3, descriptive; its Λ clock was not confirmed), and it matches summed learning rate in one confirmed equivalence cell (lr × 0.25) and is consistent with it in a second (lr × 2: direction confirmed, equality descriptive) once Adam's moment windows are rescaled (R9, addition mod 113, π measure; Appendix D). Under minibatches the learning-rate effect depended on the batch size (N54b), so no single summed-learning-rate clock holds there. (v) *Horizon:* switch experiments are read at most ≈ 5000 steps after the switch (full batch 2000–4000), other final models at 2000–12 000 steps; much longer training is untested, and representation metrics measured at grokking need not be converged; for example, effective rank kept compressing for tens of thousands of steps after generalization (Khanh 2026b). (vi) *Design history:* many decisions were informed by pilots on seeds that were already used, and each registration lists them. Every confirmation used fresh reserved seeds and a frozen analysis manifest or code gate. Post hoc statements (e.g. energy direction, scalar Adam estimate, equal-energy test) are not confirmations.

Positive in 50/50 seeds in every task.

Arms of one unit share initialization and test set and are joined by grey lines. E1, E2, E8: engineered splits with steering strength ε = 1, 2, 8 (E2 for target sets A and B, E1 and E8 for A); random R: uniform split of the same size; control D: same number of training pairs per output value as its E2 split, positions uniform within each anti-diagonal. Black bars: medians. Geometric-mean ratios R/E2(A) ×6.5 [5.3, 7.9] and D/E2 ×7.5 [6.5, 8.6] (mean over both target sets), same direction in 20/20 units; bounded times make both ratios conservative.

*Figure 3.* **The choice starts to persist within 25–50 steps (addition mod 113).** Left, top: switch cost C(t) = log2 of the time to test accuracy ≥ 0.95 (counted from step 0, bounded at 2000) after t steps on one engineered split and then on a pair-disjoint split with other targets, relative to training on the destination split only; mean over both directions, 95 % bootstrap CI over 30 fresh seeds (R6). C > 0: the switch delays grokking (t = 10–40). At t = 50 and 75 the mean is negative (−0.40, 24/30 seeds; −1.33, 30/30): the switched run reaches the threshold earlier than the destination-only run, while its final embedding energy stays close to that of the source split (median π ≈ 1). Left, bottom: median persistence π(t) of the same runs (the mean π = 0.351 in Section 5 is from the separate block P3) (0 = final embedding like the destination split alone, 1 = like the source split alone; affine index, can exceed 1). Right: cost of a switch at t = 25 to other targets (A↔B) and to the same targets with new pairs (A↔A2), each the mean of both directions, 25 fresh seeds (R8); lines join the two values of a seed. Several switch runs had not generalized by step 2000 (A→B 20/25, B→A 15/25 did; same-target switches 24/25 each), so these costs are bounded.

*Figure 4.* **Minibatch training: steering holds, lock-in comes later (addition mod 113; confirmed blocks only).** (a) L0, 10 fresh seeds: Δ_pow at the end of the 30 000-step budget under i.i.d. minibatches of 256 and 64 (dots: seeds; black: mean with the frozen 95 % CI; solid line: 0, no steering; the registered criterion was Δ_pow > 0). At batch 64, 12 of 20 runs ended the budget below 0.99 training accuracy (minimum 0.79; post hoc). (b) N54b, 10 fresh seeds: mean persistence π(t) of the final embedding after a switch at step t, per batch size, learning rate 10⁻³ (solid) and 2·10⁻³ (dashed); the dotted line marks the half-point 0.5. (c) Half-point t½ per seed (circles 10⁻³, triangles 2·10⁻³) against the steps per epoch N/B (log–log), with the mean slopes α (10⁻³ frozen hypothesis; 2·10⁻³ secondary); lines join the means. The slope is an average over N/B = 3.7–60; log t½ is curved. Drawn by `figures/fig13_minibatch_confirmed.py` from `L0_summary.json` and `N54B_summary.json`. The order-against-set pilot (former Figure 4, `fig11_l0_set_vs_order.py`) moves to Appendix I.

## Appendix A: Robustness (R1/C1, P4/C3, R7, R2/C2)

#### A.1 K2 holds across learning rate, weight decay and train fraction (R1, manifest 6298e67); mask-spectrum order of the targets (C1)

*Registered before any run; six cells, each changing exactly one hyperparameter from the preset (lr 1e-3, weight decay 1, train fraction 0.3); 15 fresh seeds per cell (2420–2509), F/G pairs with a shared initialization as in P1, add 113, 2000 steps, GPU; for the train-fraction cells ε was calibrated beforehand on separate calibration seeds so that the mask target share equals the preset's; session 37.*
Δ_pow at step 2000 (mean, 95 % bootstrap CI; exact one-sided sign-flip test, Holm over the six cells; every cell 15/15 seeds positive, Holm-p 1.8·10⁻⁴, no technical failures; registered threshold: Holm-p < 0.05 and lower CI bound ≥ 1):

| Cell | Δ_pow (95 % CI) | arms generalized by step 2000 (trainer-logged generalization event) | median test accuracy at step 2000 |
|---|---|---|---|
| lr 5·10⁻⁴ | 5.81 [5.43, 6.18] | 23/30 | 1.00 |
| lr 2·10⁻³ | 9.37 [8.94, 9.79] | 30/30 | 1.00 |
| weight decay 0.3 | 4.30 [4.13, 4.46] | 5/30 | 0.57 |
| weight decay 3 | 10.74 [9.96, 11.41] | 29/30 | 1.00 |
| train fraction 0.2 | 4.80 [4.58, 5.04] | 2/30 | 0.28 |
| train fraction 0.5 | 9.11 [8.63, 9.57] | 30/30 | 1.00 |

The steering holds in every cell. Its size varies (preset, P1: 8.24) and is smallest in the two cells where few runs had generalized by step 2000, consistent with the post hoc observation that Δ_pow keeps growing after generalization (Appendix F); cells differ in training progress at a fixed step count, so this is not a phase-matched comparison (registered estimand: steering after 2000 optimizer steps). *Post hoc (session 44, exploration on seen data; `lab/confirm/R1_posthoc_lrwd_time_s44.py`, supplementary figure `lab/paper/figures/fig12_r1_lrwd_time.py`):* with decoupled weight decay a natural time is τ = t·lr·wd (the decay shrinks the weights by 1 − lr·wd per step; AdamW weights as an exponential moving average of recent updates, Wang & Aitchison, ICML 2025, arXiv 2405.13698; the grokking time scale is set by lr·wd, generalization time ∝ 1/(lr·wd), Pracher et al. 2026, arXiv 2609.26679). Read at τ, the seed-mean Δ_pow of the four lr/wd cells lies closer to the preset curve than at equal steps: mean |log ratio| 0.134 against 0.349 over all 22 available points (τ ≤ 2000), so the reading fixed before the computation was only “partial”. The misfit sits at τ < 250, where the preset curve is only known at steps 0 and 250; with these points excluded (post hoc) it is 0.038 (18 points, largest 0.073) against 0.38. Small systematic residuals remain (lr 5·10⁻⁴ +5 to +8 % at every point with τ ≥ 250; lr 2·10⁻³ drifting to −4 %). The R1 cells and P1 use different seeds and splits (same construction, ε = 2); the preset curve is the mean of the 50 P1 seeds on a 250-step grid, interpolated linearly. The points are successive readings of 4 cells, lr and wd were never changed together, and the early phase is untested (both prepared as EXP-103). So, after this post hoc exclusion, most of the size differences between these R1 cells are captured by a rescaling of time by lr·wd in this range; the small learning-rate-specific residuals above remain (see the follow-up below). This concerns the growth of Δ_pow, not the lock-in clock of R3/R9 (Appendix D.1, Appendix D.2). *Follow-up (EXP-103, session 46, exploration, readings fixed before the runs; not independently recomputed):* a dense preset curve removed the interpolation gap for three of the four early points, but not for the earliest (wd 0.3 at τ = 75: |log ratio| 0.73, the cell lying above the preset, 2.80 against 1.35; still 0.14 when read in summed learning rate; pre-set reading “unclear”); the three other points keep offsets of +5 to +7 %. Two cells with equal lr·wd but different lr (2·10⁻³/0.5 against 5·10⁻⁴/2, 10 seeds) each stay close to the preset curve (lr·wd = 10⁻³) from t = 250 to 2000 (mean |log ratio| 0.044 and 0.049; pre-set reading “product form holds”, threshold 0.10), but on opposite sides of it at every step from 250 on (signed mean −0.044 and +0.049; paired log ratio at step 2000 −0.09 [−0.13, −0.05] and +0.07 [0.01, 0.15]), and they differ strongly before (descriptive, as fixed before the runs): paired difference in Δ_pow +1.83 [1.73, 1.94] at t = 100, +1.18 at 150, +0.34 at 200 (10/10 each). So from about 250 steps on the rescaling by lr·wd describes the steering to within the pre-set tolerance of 10 %, with small systematic learning-rate-dependent offsets; earlier, the larger learning rate steers sooner at equal lr·wd.
*C1 (separate family, code gate 96380b2 committed before the R1 manifest):* within each arm, the rank order of the five targets by W_E energy at step 2000 follows their rank in the centred coherent mask spectrum M0c of the split: S = 0.45 [0.39, 0.52] (equal-weight mean of the six cell means of per-seed Spearman ρ; bootstrap CI stratified by cell), Monte-Carlo sign-flip p ≤ 5·10⁻⁶ (resolution of 200 000 flips); adjusted for frequency index and initial rank 0.45 [0.38, 0.51]; cell means 0.35–0.62. Descriptively, the uncentred M0 gives 0.35 and the initial rank 0.22. A correlation, not a mechanism; C1 makes no claim that M0c is better than M0.

#### A.2 K2 holds in a shared-embedding MLP, at 4× width and for non-modular integer addition (P4, manifest 96503bfd); mask-spectrum order of the targets there (C3)

*Registered after the pilots EXP-045 (MLP), EXP-049 (width) and EXP-048 (integer addition), 10 known seeds each (named in the registration), frozen before any run; n = 15 fresh seeds per condition (from 2360–2419, disjoint between conditions); GPU; session 38.*
Per seed, two engineered splits F and G with disjoint target sets, Δ_pow as in Section 3; exact one-sided sign-flip permutation test over all 2¹⁵ sign patterns (registered in place of the draft's t-test), Holm over the three conditions, bootstrap CI, confirmed if Holm-p < 0.05 and CI lower bound ≥ 1. **(a) MLP with a shared embedding** (add 113, Δ_pow at step 10 000, after grokking): **8.89** [7.86, 9.84]; **(b) one-layer transformer with d = 512** (4× width, add 113, step 2000): **7.84** [7.23, 8.38]; **(c) non-modular integer addition** a + b with 225 outputs (own split construction, detrended Δ_pow at step 2000): **2.35** [2.05, 2.72]. Each 15/15 seeds positive, Holm-p 9.2·10⁻⁵ (the smallest value the procedure yields at n = 15 with all signs positive), no technical failures. All MLP and d = 512 arms generalized (median test accuracy 1.0); **no** integer-addition arm generalized within 2000 steps (median test accuracy 0.26), so in (c) the steering of the W_E spectrum is shown without generalization. Secondary: MLP at step 2000 2.35, integer addition on the raw spectrum 2.24.
*Fine order (C3, own family, analysis code frozen before the P4 manifest):* in the equally weighted mean over the three conditions, the order of the five targets in W_E energy at step 2000 follows their order in the mask spectrum (coherent variant M0c for the MLP and d = 512, M0 for integer addition; choice informed by the pilots), S = **0.30** [0.20, 0.40] (Monte-Carlo sign flips, 200 000 draws, none as large: p ≤ 5·10⁻⁶; adjusted for k and the initial rank 0.30 [0.19, 0.40]; condition means 0.27, 0.31, 0.32) → confirmed. Descriptively, the rank correlation of the targets' initial and step-2000 energies is 0.54 in the MLP, −0.02 at d = 512 and 0.00 for integer addition: in the MLP the initial order correlates more strongly with the step-2000 order (0.54) than the mask order does in that condition (condition mean 0.27; descriptive, two different statistics, not tested; C3 makes no per-condition claim); the confirmed claim is the pooled, init-adjusted one. For integer addition the initial-rank control is the raw step-0 spectrum (the trainer does not store a detrended one).
**Limits:** one depth per architecture here (two layers: pilot EXP-078 and R7, Appendix A.3); the MLP value is measured after grokking, the others at step 2000; integer addition does not generalize in this budget, so its frequencies are a representation property, not a shown part of a working algorithm.

#### A.3 K2 holds in a two-layer transformer at equal step count (R7, manifest 6e2d8070)

*Registered before the pilot EXP-078 was run (known seeds 1000–1009; the design was made symmetric so that any pilot outcome would be tested), frozen after the pilot with n = 10 from a rule that simulates the registered double criterion at half the pilot mean; fresh seeds 2900–2909; same P1 splits construction and Δ_pow as Section 3, W_E of a two-layer transformer without LayerNorm; GPU; session 38.*
At step 2000 the two-layer model's W_E followed the split: Δ_pow = **6.15** [5.86, 6.47] (10/10 seeds; exact one-sided sign-flip test over all 2¹⁰ patterns, p = 2⁻¹⁰ ≈ 0.001; CI lower bound above the minimum effect 1) → **confirmed**; no technical failures. Secondary: 9.98 [9.55, 10.36] at step 10 000; paired against a one-layer run of the same seed, splits and W_E initialization at step 2000 the two-layer value was lower by 2.70 [2.18, 3.16] (0/10 higher); all two-layer arms generalized by step 10 000 (three of the 20 only after step 2000). The pilot (5.84; −2.42 against one layer) transferred.
**Limits:** "at equal step count"; the bootstrap bounds are slightly anticonservative at n = 10 and the exact test covers only Δ_pow > 0, not the minimum effect (irrelevant here with a lower bound of 5.86); only the embedding is measured (frequencies in the second layer are not); one task (add 113); no data switch, so lock-in (K4) in two layers is open.

#### A.4 The reversal of Appendix C.2 holds at double learning rate but only partly at 0.3× weight decay (R2, manifest 40a577c3); the old targets keep their order (C2)

*Registered after N29 and EXP-039 (named in the registration), frozen before any run; 30 fresh seeds (2510–2539); N29 protocol (both directions, 4000 steps after the switch, ablation contrasts of Appendix C.2, minimum difference 0.3; one-sided t-test, Holm over 4, bootstrap CI; confirmed = Holm-p < 0.05 and CI lower bound ≥ 0), with the changed hyperparameter kept for the whole run; all seeds count, generalized or not; GPU; session 38.*
**Learning rate 2·10⁻³:** holding after a switch at 50 steps, 0.97 (0.67 [0.64, 0.69] above the minimum difference; 30/30), and switching after a switch at 12 steps, 0.61 (0.31 [0.22, 0.41] above; 26/30 above 0.3), were both confirmed (Holm-p 7·10⁻²⁹ and 3.6·10⁻⁷). **Weight decay 0.3:** holding after 50 steps was confirmed (0.83; 0.53 [0.47, 0.59] above; 30/30), switching after 25 steps was **not** (0.18; −0.12 [−0.18, −0.07]; 5/30 above 0.3). At 0.3× weight decay the networks switched at step 25 mostly did not generalize within the 4000 further steps (base test accuracy ≥ 0.9 in 2/30 and 5/30 runs per direction, medians 0.34 and 0.46; after a switch at 50: 24/30 and 25/30), so this contrast there mostly describes non-generalized networks. By the registered rule the transition is robust at double learning rate and **not** robust at 0.3× weight decay (its switching side was not confirmed); only the holding side was confirmed there. No technical failures.
*Order of the old targets (C2, own family, analysis code frozen before the R2 manifest):* after a switch at 50 steps (both cells, both directions), the energy order of the five old targets in the final embedding follows their order at the switch: mean Spearman **0.61** [0.54, 0.68], 0.45 [0.38, 0.51] above a non-target control, adjusted coefficient (least squares on centered ranks, controlling k and the second split's spectrum) 0.60 [0.53, 0.66]; 30/30 seeds positive; Monte-Carlo sign flips p ≤ 5·10⁻⁶ → confirmed. The lock-in thus preserves the order within the old target set, not only the set (descriptive persistence, no mechanism).
*Time (fixed before the runs, descriptive, outside the family):* with b = min(first test accuracy ≥ 0.95, 4000), an earlier switch cost more time than a switch at 50 also here: 0.3× weight decay @25 vs @50 +1.34 log2 (29 of 29 untied seeds; b is censored at 4000 in 54/60 runs @25 and 11/60 @50 (10 of the 11 paired with a censored @25 run, 1 not), so the size is not a strict bound; the sign test supports the direction), learning rate 2·10⁻³ @12 vs @50 +2.03 (30/30), and @25 vs @50 +1.47 (30/30; not a clock test, since the learning rate stays doubled after the switch).
**Limits:** one task (add 113); two hyperparameter values; the weight-decay result is confounded with slower grokking.

## Appendix B: Functional measures and their limit (P2d/P2e)

#### B.1 Functional sensitivity along the steered frequencies (K2-function; P2d c0cd65f, P2e 3c484ef)

A one-sided step of norm 0.02·‖X‖_F (X = number rows of W_E) along the steered frequencies reduced the mean correct-class logit margin on pairs outside both splits more than the mean of four pre-specified control sets:
add 113 (4000 steps) 0.250 [0.229, 0.270], 20/20 seeds; mul 113 (8000 steps) 0.291 [0.268, 0.308]; add 97 (8000 steps) 0.294 [0.275, 0.312], each 20/20 (Holm over the two tasks).
**Limit:** in the add-113 switch models examined (EXP-064 post hoc, EXP-068; 80 N29 models), sensitivity goes along with the energy distribution in W_E; at equal removed energy the dominant set has no
advantage, but that measure changes the relative dose (exploration). P2d/P2e models were not tested with the equal-energy measure. We therefore do not claim use
beyond energy. Earlier registered functional variants were not evaluable (P2), aborted for a design error (P2b), or not confirmed with the sign reversed (P2c, loss after removing half the control energy); we report all three.

## Appendix C: Lock-in in detail (K4/K4b, K4c, resets K4d/K4e, R6/R8)

#### C.1 Early lock-in under a data switch (K4, K4b; P3 f8adf45, N28 fa154bd)

After 25 steps on a first engineered split and 2000 steps on a pair-disjoint second split, final models sat at 0.351 of the normalized log-energy distance between the two pure endpoints (the persistence index π, P3); the excess over
any tested static additive W_E trace was 0.293 [0.263, 0.322] (30 fresh seeds, 30/30). In the separate block N28 (30 other fresh seeds, same π and protocol; π = 0.340 at t = 25), zeroing Adam's first moment at the switch lowered π by 0.151 (0.340 → 0.189); ten extra
pre-switch steps with the same reset compensated this (non-inferiority, margin 0.05). This is compatible with a "pre-switch exposure" reading (longer exposure to the source split), not a proof of it. *Size, post hoc:* in a scalar
model of bias-corrected Adam (β = 0.9/0.98), the first moment at the switch still carries 6.5–10.8 update-equivalents (at t = 25–35) of displacement along the old direction (≈ 8.7–8.9 if later gradients on the
same coordinate keep their magnitude); in the pilot π curve (EXP-059, 10 known seeds, sampled every 5 steps up to t = 35), zeroing m shifted π by 8.1, 9.6 and 6.5 steps at t = 25, 30, 35, (at t = 40 and 50 the interpolated shifts, 3.8 and 2.4, are not interpretable: the curve was not sampled between 35 and 50 and approaches its natural ceiling π ≈ 1).
*Counter-pressure, post hoc (session 33, split files and the frozen P3 summary only):* at ω = 0 the second split's first-order W_E gradient at the old targets points against the first split's (projection −0.38 of the first split's own push, Section 2); at P3's secondary level ω = 0.4 this term almost vanishes (−0.02); presumably the uniformly drawn shared pairs add a common component to both splits that offsets the negative image (not decomposed). Persistence did not differ detectably (no equivalence test; π 0.351 vs 0.355; the registered secondary difference 0.005 [−0.030, 0.042]; per-seed Spearman correlation of the two changes 0.11; `lab/confirm/p3_opposition_vs_pi_s33.py`). So persistence at t = 25 showed no detectable dependence on this first-order counter-pressure, which is computed at initialization, not at the switch (the interval allows about ±0.04). The two levels also differ in ε (2.23 vs 5.93) and in the shared pairs, so this is a reading, not a controlled test.
That the first moment carries a source signal past the removal of the source data has been shown by state surgery in a different setting (Xu 2026); that fixed-clock first-moment memory makes data-order effects first order in the learning rate has been shown for fine-tuning (Sweeney 2026); a measure of training memory that grows with momentum collapses when the optimizer state is reset (Sevetlidis and Pavlidis 2026). What we add is only the size estimate in our setting.

#### C.2 An ablation contrast reverses between a switch at 25 and at 50 steps (K4c; N29 087e042)

Removing all five target frequencies from W_E after a switch and 4000 further steps: after a switch at t = 50, removing the **old** targets cost 0.903 more test accuracy than removing the new ones
(95 % CI 0.846–0.953; 20/20 seeds > 0.3); after a switch at t = 25, removing the **new** targets cost 0.603 more (0.498–0.700; 17/20 > 0.3). Two time points bracket a reversal of this ablation contrast;
a network-wide or irreversible functional commitment is not shown. Post hoc, the W_E energy points in the same direction (38/40 and 40/40 directions), so this contrast does not separate reliance
from energy. 19/20 seeds generalized; restricted to them (descriptive, part of the frozen analysis) the contrasts are 0.898 and 0.591 (16/19 > 0.3 at t = 25).

#### C.3 Reset sensitivity: attention more than the tested MLP reset, value path more than query/key (K4d N29b db31564, K4e N29c 3c9cb63)

At a switch after 50 steps, resetting W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O to initialization together with their AdamW state lowered the ablation contrast by 1.49 [1.36, 1.61] vs no reset and by 1.42 [1.28, 1.56] vs the
tested MLP reset (20 paired seeds, Holm-p 4.7·10⁻¹²). Resetting only W_V, W_O lowered it by 0.850 [0.685, 0.998] vs no reset and by 0.752 [0.596, 0.897] vs an equal-size reset of W_Q, W_K
(Holm-p 2.1·10⁻⁴ and 1.9·10⁻⁵). Arm means of the contrast (descriptive): N29b no reset 0.86, attention reset −0.63 [−0.73, −0.52], MLP reset 0.79; N29c no reset 0.81, W_V/W_O reset −0.04, W_Q/W_K reset 0.72. N29, N29b and N29c use different fresh seed sets, so their no-reset levels (0.90, 0.86, 0.81) are separate estimates of the same condition. Restricted to generalized seeds (descriptive, frozen analysis) the four differences are 1.52, 1.45, 0.805 and 0.738. These show *reset sensitivity*, not a storage location: weights and optimizer state were reset together, the VO and QK resets are matched only in parameter count, and the MLP control resets twice as many parameters and is not matched in displacement or dynamics. Generalized seeds: 19/20 (N29b),
17/20 (N29c). *Relation to prior work:* in language models the ordering is reversed (query–key reset restores, value reset does not; Dong 2026); we report our ordering for this
setting only. A possible reading (untested): our switch keeps the task and hence the routing requirement (attend to both operands) and changes only which frequencies the
content carries, which passes through the value/output path; a withheld capability in a language model plausibly requires new routing (query–key).
*Is the stronger reset simply the one that removes more movement? (exploration EXP-083, seen seeds, reading fixed before the runs; session 39):* we re-ran the first 50 steps of every N29b/N29c seed and split (gated: initialization checksums and W_E at steps 0 and 50 equal to the frozen block's snapshots within 10⁻³) and measured ‖W(50) − W(0)‖_F per reset part, i.e. the weight displacement each reset undoes (the optimizer state it also clears is not measured). The query/key reset removes *more* than the value/output reset, in absolute terms (7.41 vs 5.70) and relative to the part's initial norm (0.46 vs 0.36), in 20/20 seeds each, yet it has the smaller effect; for this pair a pure weight-displacement explanation is contradicted. For attention vs MLP the two scales disagree (the MLP reset removes more in absolute terms, 9.82 vs 9.37; attention more relative to its norm, 0.41 vs 0.39; each 20/20), so that pair stays unclear.

#### C.4 A data switch inside the lock-in window delays grokking, much more when the target frequencies change (R6, manifest 5b2bca6; R8, manifest d79f97d)

*Registered after post hoc reads of N28/P3/EXP-020/EXP-041/EXP-056/EXP-059 (named in the registration), frozen before any run; 30 fresh seeds (2800–2829), N28 construction (ω = 0), per seed pure A, pure B and switches A→B, B→A at t ∈ {10, 20, 25, 30, 40, 50, 75} (t + 2000 steps, AdamW state kept), GPU; session 37.*
With b = min(first test accuracy ≥ 0.95, 2000) counted from step 0 and C(t) the mean over both directions of log2 b(switch at t) − log2 b(destination split only), a switch at t = 25 delayed grokking:
C(25) = +0.85 log2 [0.73, 0.96] (a factor ≈ 1.8; 29/30 seeds; Holm-p 5.8·10⁻⁸), and more than a switch at t = 50: C(25) − C(50) = +1.25 [0.97, 1.50] (28/30; Holm-p 4.3·10⁻⁷)
(p = max of the exact sign-flip and the exact sign test, Holm over the two hypotheses; bootstrap CIs). Across the grid (mean C; seeds with C > 0): t = 10 +0.54 (28/30), 20 +0.88 (30/30), 25 +0.85 (29/30), 30 +0.67 (28/30), 40 +0.27 (22/30), 50 −0.40 (6/30), 75 −1.33 (0/30).
The median persistence π(t) of the same runs crosses 0.5 at t_π = 31; the registered secondary S1 (largest cost within 10 steps of t_π) was **not supported** (largest mean cost at t = 20, 11 steps away), S2 (cost ≤ 0 wherever median π ≥ 0.9 and > 0 wherever 0.2 ≤ π ≤ 0.8) was supported. Switch runs without an event by step 2000 count at the bound (27/60 at t = 20, 18/60 at t = 25, 1/60 at t = 50; destination-only runs 0/60), so these costs are lower bounds and the location of the largest cost is uncertain.
*Descriptive, fixed before the runs:* at t = 25, 94 % of the delay lies in the gap between memorizing the destination split and generalizing (38 of the 42 of 60 direction pairs in which both events occurred have a larger gap delay); after a switch at t = 50 (registered prediction, sign test p = 9.3·10⁻¹⁰), test accuracy at the moment the new split is memorized exceeds that of the destination-only run at the same step by +0.22 (30/30); at t = 25 (descriptive only) by −0.04 (4/30). As a reading: after 50 steps the new split is fitted through already fixed features.
**Limits:** each arm has exactly 2000 updates up to the horizon, so C(t) compares regimes: t destination updates are replaced by source updates. Fewer destination updates alone could raise C (more distinct pairs could lower it). The confirmed H2 argues against a reading in which the cost only reflects fewer destination updates, which predicts C(50) ≥ C(25); no mixed A∪B control was run. In the pilot EXP-086 (Appendix F; seen seeds, and A2 carries new, partly reversed wave phases, so a phase conflict is not excluded) a switch to a pair-disjoint split with the *same* targets did not cost time; its confirmation R8 is reported below. Qualitatively, that the cost of earlier training for a new task depends on how the tasks relate is known from critical-period analyses in deep linear networks (Kleinman, Achille and Soatto 2024). Time to a threshold is a coarse measure (evaluated every 25 steps).

*Is the cost specific to a change of target frequencies? (R8, manifest d79f97d; registered after the pilot EXP-086, frozen before any run; n = 25 fresh seeds 3100–3124 from a power rule over a bootstrap and a normal model; session 37.)* Per seed, besides A and B, a split A2 was built that carries the **same** five targets as A with matched steering strength (realised mask share on the targets within 0.005 of A), is pair-disjoint from A and drawn from the same pool, but has new, partly reversed wave phases (about a quarter of its first-order target power lies along −A, as for B; EXP-086). A switch at t = 25 from A to A2 (and back) did not delay grokking on average (not tested against 0): C_AA2 = −0.15 log2 (8/25 seeds positive), whereas the switch to the other targets did: C_AB = +0.66 (24/25; censored at 2000 like R6: A→B 20/25 and B→A 15/25 runs generalized by then, the same-target switches 24/25 each, so both costs are lower bounds). The registered primary difference D = C_AB − C_AA2 = +0.81 log2 [0.57, 1.04] (24/25; p = max(exact sign-flip, exact sign test) = 1.7·10⁻⁶); the registered secondary C_AA2 < ½·C_AB was supported (difference −0.48 [−0.64, −0.32]). The pilot value (+0.82 on 10 seen seeds) transferred. So the delay is not a generic cost of an early change of the training pairs, nor of fewer destination updates alone (A→A2 replaces as many destination updates as A→B): it is much larger with a different target set (t = 25). This parallels the observation that early deficits which leave the low-level input statistics unchanged have no lasting effect in image networks (Achille et al. 2019); here the analogue is controlled at matched steering strength and measured as time to generalization. **Limit:** a split with A's own wave phases and matched strength that is disjoint from A cannot be built from the same pool (EXP-086), so a pure phase conflict is not excluded; one task (add 113) and one architecture.

## Appendix D: The clock of the lock-in (R3, R9/K5, R10, R11)

#### D.1 Summed learning rate versus step count: a pure step clock does not fit, the Λ clock is not confirmed (R3, manifest 51b117f6)

*Registered after N29, the pilot EXP-039 (known seeds, "unclear") and EXP-059 (named in the registration), frozen before any run; 20 fresh seeds (2540–2559), N29 protocol (ω = 0, both directions, 4000 steps after the switch, ablation of the 5 old or 5 new target frequencies from W_E on the held-out test set, mean over both directions); the learning rate is scaled by c only in steps 1 … t on the first split and is the default from the switch on; GPU; session 38.*
Two cells separate a clock in summed learning rate Λ = c·t (in units of default steps) from a clock in steps: lr × 2 for t = 25 (Λ = 50) and lr × 0.5 for t = 50 (Λ = 25). The Λ clock predicts holding in the first and switching in the second, the step clock the opposite. With the Appendix C.2 contrasts and minimum difference 0.3 (one-sided t-test, Holm over 2, bootstrap CI), **holding after 25 steps at double learning rate was confirmed**: removing the old targets cost 0.70 more than removing the new ones, 0.40 [0.27, 0.51] above the minimum difference (20/20 seeds > 0, 18/20 > 0.3; Holm-p 5.4·10⁻⁶). **Switching after 50 steps at half learning rate was not confirmed**: the reverse contrast was 0.32, only 0.02 [−0.09, 0.14] above the minimum difference (18/20 > 0, 9/20 > 0.3; Holm-p 0.37). The registered reading is therefore **"Λ clock not confirmed"**. Neither cell fits the step clock (registered descriptive reading, no test): no seed reached the minimum difference in the step-clock direction (0/20 in each cell; at half learning rate 2/20 seeds leaned slightly that way, by ≤ 0.03). All 20 seeds generalized; no technical failures.
So the time of lock-in does not follow the step count alone: relative to the default values of N29 (other seeds; R3 has no default arm), doubling the early learning rate appears to bring it forward and halving it to delay it, both in the direction Λ predicts; in magnitude the double-learning-rate cell passed the registered bar and the half-learning-rate cell did not (post hoc, relative to the N29 values at t = 25 and 50 from other seeds, the two cells lie about 86 % and 81 % of the way from the step-clock to the Λ-clock expectation). **Limits:** two cells, one task (add 113); the registration names alternatives that scale like Λ in these cells without Λ being the mechanism (Adam's step-dependent moments and bias correction, larger early steps overshooting), and the shortfall from the Λ expectation in both cells (post hoc; the registered test failed only at half learning rate) is compatible with such a mixed clock. Pilots after R3 (Appendix F) suggest that this shortfall comes from Adam's moment windows (β₁ and β₂ rescaled together), which are fixed in steps: with the betas rescaled so that the windows are equal in summed learning rate, the step dependence was not detectable (+0.002 [−0.024, 0.024]; EXP-090, one Λ and c = 0.25; exploration), and at lr × 2 the rescaling moved lock-in toward the Λ expectation (EXP-091, pilot on seen seeds). The R3 cells themselves (c = 2 and 0.5, accuracy measure) were not re-tested. The window rule was then confirmed on fresh seeds in two other cells (c = 0.25 and c = 2) with the π measure of Appendix F (R9, Appendix D.2).

#### D.2 Rescaling Adam's moment windows to summed learning rate removes most of the step dependence of lock-in (equivalent at lr × 0.25, direction confirmed at lr × 2; R9, manifest 8b22879a)

*Registered after R3 (Appendix D.1) and the pilots EXP-081, EXP-089, EXP-090 and EXP-091 (Appendix F; named in the registration with the decisions they informed: Λ = 25 with t = 100, the β rescaling rule, the equivalence margin ±0.1, c = 2 with t = 15, and testing H3 against 0), design and code checked by an independent read-only agent before freezing (after which H1 was changed from a test against the minimum effect 0.05 to a test against 0 and n raised from 24 to 36 by a power simulation with Holm and the CI rule); frozen before any run; 36 fresh seeds (3300–3335); GPU; session 40.*
Protocol as in Appendix F (EXP-089/090): add 113, one-layer transformer, pair-disjoint ω = 0 split pairs built from each seed, a switch A → B and B → A after t steps, then 2000 steps at the default learning rate and betas; π = persistence of the old choice in the log energy ratio of W_E group power, from the final embedding against pure A and B runs of the same seed, averaged over both directions. Before the switch the learning rate is scaled by c, so that Λ = c·t in default steps; in the rescaled arms the betas are also changed before the switch to β′ = 1 − c(1 − β), which makes Adam's moment windows equal in Λ (1 − β′ = c(1 − β); β′ = 0.975/0.995 for c = 0.25 and 0.8/0.96 for c = 2). Per seed 14 runs: pure A/B, default t = 25 and t = 30, (c = 0.25, t = 100) with default and rescaled betas, (c = 2, t = 15) with default and rescaled betas. Family of three, Holm, one-sided paired t-tests, 95 % bootstrap CIs over seeds.
**H1 (direction at c = 0.25, Λ = 25):** e₁ = π(default β) − π(β′) = **+0.161** [0.132, 0.192] (36/36 seeds > 0; Holm-p 3·10⁻¹²; confirmed = Holm-p < 0.05 and CI lower bound > 0; the lower bound is also above the originally planned minimum effect 0.05, descriptive). **H2 (equivalence at Λ = 25):** d₁ = π(c = 0.25, t = 100, β′) − π(default, t = 25) = **+0.015** [0.005, 0.027] (TOST against ±0.1, Holm-p 3·10⁻¹⁶). **H3 (second level, c = 2, Λ = 30):** e₂ = π(β′) − π(default β) = **+0.057** [0.042, 0.073] (34/36; Holm-p 1.5·10⁻⁸; per-seed values in supplementary figure `lab/paper/figures/fig9_r9_window_clock.py`). All three confirmed; registered reading **"window rule confirmed"**. 36/36 seeds valid (none excluded for too small a gap between the pure runs); one run failed technically in the first pass (a Windows file-access error when renaming its result file) and was recomputed and bound in a second pass of the same job list.
*Descriptive (outside the family):* d₂ = π(c = 2, t = 15, β′) − π(default, t = 30) = −0.007 [−0.021, 0.009]. Arm means of π (post hoc): default t = 25 0.34, t = 30 0.44; c = 0.25 0.51 with default and 0.35 with rescaled betas; c = 2 0.38 with default and 0.44 with rescaled betas. The separation of the two frequency sets in W_E at the switch (0.034 / 0.052 / 0.035 for t = 25 / c = 0.25 default / c = 0.25 rescaled; 0.047 / 0.039 / 0.046 for t = 30 / c = 2 default / c = 2 rescaled), which does not depend on Adam's step counter, points the same way; the rescaled c = 0.25 arm keeps 0.06 of the gap between the unrescaled arm and t = 25.
So, consistent with the deviation from a pure Λ clock seen in Appendix D.1 (whose cells were not re-tested), the deviation runs in both directions as a moment lag counted in steps predicts (R9 rescaled both betas; the pilots EXP-090 and EXP-081 point to the first moment): with fewer, larger steps (c = 2) the default windows are longer in Λ and lock-in is weaker than Λ predicts; with more, smaller steps (c = 0.25) they are shorter and lock-in is stronger; rescaling the betas so that the windows are equal in Λ reduces the difference to about a tenth in both cells (at c = 0.25 from 0.18 to 0.015, equivalent within ±0.1; at c = 2 from −0.06 to −0.007, descriptive). The rescaling 1 − β′ = c(1 − β) is the deterministic continuous-time matching in which 1 − β shrinks in proportion to the step size (the regime of the continuous-time analysis of Adam by Barakat & Bianchi, arXiv 1810.02263, Assumption 2.5: (1 − β(γ))/γ tends to a constant as the step size γ → 0); it differs from Malladi et al.'s SDE square-root rule (2022, Definition 5.2: η′ = √κ·η and 1 − β′ = κ(1 − β), i.e. 1 − β′ = c²(1 − β) in terms of the learning-rate factor c), which matches gradient noise across batch sizes. That Adam's first moment is a memory on a fixed step clock, which makes data-order effects first order in the learning rate, has been shown for fine-tuning (Sweeney 2026, arXiv 2606.29554). R9 is therefore an application of known optimization principles; what is tested here is their consequence for the persistence of the early frequency choice.
**Limits:** one task (add 113), one architecture, full batch, two (c, Λ) pairs; π is a representation measure (W_E energy), no ablation; H2 means "equivalent within ±0.1 although Adam's step counter differs after the switch (100 against 25)", and the small positive rest (+0.015, CI excluding 0) is compatible with that difference; the R3 cells and its accuracy measure were not re-tested; why a shorter lag makes the early motion more frequency-selective is open.

#### D.3 Fewer gradient evaluations before a switch weaken lock-in under Adam (R10, manifest 7b583bdb)

*Registered after the pilot EXP-095 (Appendix F; named in the registration with the decisions it informed: direction, effect sizes and SDs of all three hypotheses, k = 8 and 24, the equivalence margin ±0.05) and EXP-094/EXP-093/R9 (c8b cell, Λ = 24, block design); design and code checked by an independent read-only agent before freezing; the sentences for every outcome were fixed before the result was seen ([[paper/R10_DEUTUNGEN]]); 48 fresh seeds (3500–3547); GPU; sessions 43–45.*
Protocol as R9 (Appendix D.2): add 113, pair-disjoint split pairs, switch A → B and B → A at t, then 2000 default steps, π from the final W_E group power against the pure runs of the same seed. Cells per seed: n24 (24 default Adam steps), g8 and g24 (the same 24 Adam steps, but a fresh gradient only every 8 or 24 steps, the stored one reused in between), c8b (3 steps at 8× learning rate with Λ-matched betas 0.2/0.84). Family of three, Holm, one-sided paired t-tests, 95 % bootstrap CIs over seeds; 48/48 seeds valid, none excluded, no technical failure.
**H1:** e₈ = π(n24) − π(g8) = **+0.147** [0.115, 0.181] (45/48; Holm-p 3·10⁻¹¹), confirmed. **H2 (equivalence g8 ≈ c8b within ±0.05):** r₈ = π(g8) − π(c8b) = +0.057 [0.038, 0.078] (TOST p = 0.76), **not confirmed**. **H3:** e₂₄ = π(n24) − π(g24) = **+0.234** [0.201, 0.266] (48/48; Holm-p 3·10⁻¹⁸), confirmed. Registered reading "partial: H1, H3". Cell means of π: n24 0.346, g8 0.198, c8b 0.141, g24 0.112 (descriptive).
With 24 Adam steps held fixed, fewer gradient evaluations along the path gave weaker persistence (e₈ = 0.147 [0.115, 0.181], e₂₄ = 0.234 [0.201, 0.266]; n = 48). Equivalence of 3 evaluations and 3 large steps was not shown (r₈ = 0.057 [0.038, 0.078]); the counter difference after the switch confounds this contrast. This is a property of Adam with stale gradients, which includes near-sign steps; it does not isolate fresh directional information.
**Limits:** one task (add 113), one architecture, full batch; π is a representation measure (W_E energy), no ablation; with a frozen gradient Adam takes near-sign steps (Appendix F, EXP-095), so H1/H3 do not separate staleness from sign quantisation (a separating test, EXP-097, is prepared but deferred under the week plan). The CI of r₈ lies above 0 (g8 keeps more than c8b); this is not interpreted, because the cells differ in Adam's step counter after the switch.

#### D.4 The 25–50-step lock-in generalizes to add 97 and mul 113 (π measure; R11, manifest 14621ad6)

*Registered after the pilot EXP-044 (Appendix F; named in the registration: switch steps 25/50, the thresholds 0.5 (H2/H3) and L(F) − L(G) ≥ 2, effect sizes and SDs for the power calculation); design and code checked by an independent read-only agent before freezing; frozen before any run; the same 30 fresh seeds (3620–3649) for both tasks; GPU; session 46; recomputed by an independent agent with its own code (all means equal to within 3·10⁻¹⁷); a documented overlap of random streams between split and target draws of different seeds (registration, Fassung 2) was judged negligible.*
Protocol as EXP-044: per task and seed a common held-out test set and two engineered train sets F and G with disjoint target sets (EXP-043 construction in group coordinates; mul 113 via the discrete logarithm, group Z₁₁₂); runs pure F, pure G, and F → G at t = 25 and t = 50, each followed by 2000 default steps; π(t) = (L(t) − L(G)) / (L(F) − L(G)) with L the log ratio of final W_E group power on the F and G targets. Family of six (2 tasks × 3), Holm, one-sided t-tests, 95 % bootstrap CIs; 30/30 seeds valid per task, no technical failure.
**add 97:** π(25) = 0.377, π(50) = 0.899; H1 d = π(50) − π(25) = **+0.522** [0.455, 0.589] (30/30; Holm-p 7.5·10⁻¹⁵); H2 π(50) − 0.5 = +0.399 [0.348, 0.448]; H3 0.5 − π(25) = +0.123 [0.066, 0.177] (23/30; Holm-p 1.1·10⁻⁴). **mul 113:** π(25) = 0.270, π(50) = 0.737; H1 **+0.467** [0.396, 0.540] (30/30; Holm-p 9.3·10⁻¹³); H2 +0.237 [0.171, 0.303] (27/30); H3 +0.230 [0.183, 0.275] (29/30). All six confirmed; registered reading "K4 generalizes".
So the window in which the first split's choice becomes persistent, between 25 and 50 steps at lr 10⁻³, is not specific to add 113: at 25 steps the second split wins the larger part, at 50 steps most of the first choice persists, for another prime modulus (add 97) and for multiplication mod 113, which in the discrete-log coordinate is addition in Z₁₁₂ plus a zero token.
**Limits:** π is a representation measure (W_E energy), no ablation (the functional contrast K4c was tested only at add 113); one architecture, full-batch AdamW, one switch protocol and one direction (F → G; R9/R10 average both directions).

## Appendix E: D59 (P2f, C4)

#### E.1 D59: functional sensitivity after grokking (K2-function D59; P2f 15539d8) and mask-spectrum order of the steered irreps (C4)

*Registered after the pilot EXP-072 (5 known seeds; seen data named in the registration), frozen before any P2f run; 20 fresh seeds (2340–2359), arms F and G, 12 000 steps, GPU; session 36.*
With X = the 118 group-element rows of W_E and u_S the unit direction of the projection of X onto the isotypic components of the irreps in S, a step X' = X − 0.02·‖X‖_F·u_S along the arm's own five
target irreps reduced the mean correct-class logit margin on pairs outside both splits more than the mean of four control sets of five irreps (drawn from irreps 1–29 excluding own targets, other-arm targets and fold(2k) of the own targets):
D = 0.233 [0.214, 0.253] (mean over seeds of the arm-averaged difference; 95 % bootstrap CI), t = 22.5, one-sided p = 1.8·10⁻¹⁵, 20/20 seeds positive, no technical failures (registered threshold:
p < 0.05 and lower CI bound ≥ 0.05). 17/20 seeds generalized in both arms (test accuracy ≥ 0.9) by step 12 000; restricted to them (descriptive) D = 0.243 [0.222, 0.262]. The pilot (5 known seeds, 20 000 steps) gave 0.223 ± 0.024 (SD).
The own targets carry a median (over 40 arms) of 0.98 of the energy of the 118 element rows of W_E at step 12 000 (minimum 0.63), so, as a reading, the steered targets also dominate the step-12 000 embedding in this block (on its own splits; 37/40 arms generalized).
*Secondary S1 (registered):* seeds whose own targets carry a higher share of the two-dimensional irrep power of W_E at step 2000 (mean of both arms) generalized earlier (Spearman ρ = −0.60, one-sided permutation p = 0.0035; never-generalized arms counted as 12 001, 3 arms). This is a progress-measure correlation in the spirit of Nanda et al. (2023), not a causal statement.
*C4 (separate family, code gate c8801d3 committed before P2f):* within each arm, the rank order of the five target irreps by W_E energy at step 12 000 follows their rank order in the split's mask spectrum (M0):
mean per-seed Spearman S = 0.37 [0.225, 0.51] (bootstrap CI), sign-flip p = 1.4·10⁻⁴; adjusted for irrep index and initial rank 0.36 [0.22, 0.49] (all 20 seeds; 37/40 arms generalized; registered threshold p < 0.05, lower CI bound ≥ 0.10 and adjusted lower bound > 0). A correlation, not a mechanism.
**Limit:** in the add-113 switch models examined (EXP-068; Appendix B.1), sensitivity at equal step norm went along with the energy distribution in W_E; the P2f models were not tested with the equal-energy measure, so we do not claim use beyond energy. One perturbation form, one step size, W_E only.

## Appendix F: Explorations and negative results

- Lock-in is smooth in the number of pre-switch steps (π ≈ 0.01, 0.19, 0.30, 0.56, 1.05 at t = 10, 20, 25, 35, 50; pilot, 10 known seeds); neither the W_E lead nor OV alignment at the switch predicts
  it better than the step count (EXP-060, EXP-070, EXP-071).
- *Random splits (association; crossed pilot).* For ordinary random 30 % splits of add 113 (baseline runs, seeds 10–19), the mask spectrum M0 of a run's own split ranks its final top-5 W_E frequencies better than chance and better than other runs' masks (pre-registered test decided at n = 8, seeds 10–17: mean normalized rank 0.277 vs 0.499 with foreign masks; 0.279 vs 0.492 with all 10 seeds, reported afterwards; interpreted as an association only after a later review, EXP-015). Split and initialization of these runs were drawn from identically seeded generators, so this does not separate the split from the seed; a crossed init × split pilot (EXP-014, seeds 10–19, 5 units, CPU; session 39) found no significant difference in top-5 overlap between split and initialization (registered reading "no dominant factor", p = 0.41), while the final frequencies ranked high under the mask spectrum of the *used* split and at chance under the unused split of the same initialization (mean normalized rank 0.21 vs 0.55, 5/5 pairs, p = 1/32). The registered confirmation R4 (Section 3) shows that a random split biases the choice (descriptively more than the initialization).
- The mask spectrum M0 predicts the learned frequencies (EXP-015) and is closely related, at first order, to the power of the first W_E gradient (coherent variant M0c for the transformer;
EXP-050: first order explains only part; [[BEFUND-split-mechanismus]]); it is *not* the first-stage utility of
  the simplest AGF model (EXP-076, negative).
- Post hoc on the 50 confirmed add-113 seeds of P1: the M0 target contrast of a seed's split pair correlates with the size of its Δ_pow (Spearman 0.39, permutation p 0.006; centred M0c
  0.26, p 0.07; two measures, not pre-registered); split contrasts vary little, so most of the seed-to-seed spread comes from elsewhere. In the shuffled control of EXP-047, Δ_pow is also
  ≈ 0 on the continuous measure (0.02 ± 0.65, post hoc).
- Post hoc on all P1 arms (session 28, `lab/confirm/P1_posthoc_within.py`): the order of the five targets partly follows the mask spectrum of the split. Mean within-arm Spearman
  between a target's mask-spectrum power and its W_E power at step 2000: add 113 0.44 (centred M0c) / 0.32 (M0), mul 113 0.21, add 97 0.29, D59 0.43 (M0), each p ≤ 1/20 000 by within-arm permutation (no permutation reached the observed value); the weakest learned target is the one with the lowest mask power in only 0.26–0.42 of arms (chance 0.20);
  initialization power 0.08–0.15. No dependence on the frequency index (ρ 0.008), mismatched arms ρ −0.08 (`lab/confirm/P1_posthoc_kcontrol.py`). The within-arm spread of M0c is small (median max/min 1.30 in the P1 add-113 arms and in the 180 R1 splits), so the realized pair spectrum orders
  the targets, not only selects them (not specific to the shared-path derivation: the MLP pilot shows the same M0c > M0 ordering, Appendix G). Registered for fresh data before any R1 run as C1 ([[confirm/C1_REGISTRATION|C1]]). Confirmed on R1 (Appendix A.1). The order is not a pre-grokking transient in the transformer: in the stored P2d/P2e runs (generalization at a median of 725 steps for add/mul 113) the mean within-arm ρ declines only slowly after generalization (add 113 M0c 0.54 at step 250, 0.37 at 2000, 0.42 at 4000; add 97 0.36 → 0.24 at 8000; mul 113 0.22 at step 500 → 0.13 at 8000 (not monotone; add 97 and mul 113 with M0); `lab/confirm/P2de_posthoc_time.py`), whereas in the MLP pilot it fades by step 10 000 (0.60 → 0.17). In D59 (pilot EXP-072, 5 seeds × 2 arms; first test accuracy ≥ 0.9 at a median of 4575 steps per the EXP-072 note) it stays at 0.48–0.58 from step 250 to 20 000 (`lab/confirm/EXP072_posthoc_time.py`).
- *Steering after grokking* (session 30, `lab/confirm/P2de_posthoc_dpow_time.py`; post hoc on the stored P2d/P2e runs, whose seeds were seen for K2-function but not for Δ_pow beyond step 2000): Δ_pow is positive in 20/20 seeds of every task at every stored step after initialization and keeps growing after generalization (median generalization step 725 for add/mul 113, 1225 for add 97), then levels off: add 113 7.77 [7.36, 8.18] at step 2000 → 9.44 [8.99, 9.90] at 4000; mul 113 8.33 → 9.69 [8.99, 10.29] at 8000; add 97 6.33 → 9.39 [8.89, 9.84] at 8000 (mean, 95 % bootstrap CI over seeds). The steered set is therefore not a pre-grokking transient. Decomposition (add 113, median over 40 arms): the other arm's targets fall below their initial power by step 2000 (13.0 at 500, 1.9 at 2000; init 10.0) and stay flat (1.6 at 4000), while the own targets keep growing (128 → 202; share of the W_E power 0.82 → 0.89), so the late growth of Δ_pow is carried by the own targets, not by further pruning (descriptive).
