- *Engineered splits grok much earlier (observation, post hoc, confounded).* On the same device the engineered splits reached test accuracy ≥ 0.95 (the trainer's generalization event) after a median of 662 steps (pilot EXP-016, CPU, 20 runs) versus 5975 for random splits (10 runs); in EXP-047 (same seeds, initialization, size and token frequencies) 20/20 engineered arms generalized within 2000 steps (median 688) and 0/20 arms with shuffled pair structure did. These test sets were complements of the training split. With a common held-out test set (EXP-041 runs on the EXP-018 splits, seeds 20–29, CPU, 2150 steps; not analysed for speed at the time) the engineered arm generalized in 9/10 seeds (425–1775 steps) and the uniform random arm in 0/10 (test accuracy ≤ 0.15), so test-set composition does not explain the gap. Whether spectral concentration rather than any structured non-uniformity is responsible was tested by the pre-registered pilot EXP-018 with a control whose sampling weights are permuted within each antidiagonal (matched in weights, not exactly in the realized per-output counts, which differ by ≈ 3 of ≈ 34 pairs; result below; its engineered and random arms were already seen through EXP-041). This would run against the frequency-principle expectation that a training spectrum mismatched to the test set delays generalization (Zhou, Zhang and Xu 2024). That the choice of training data changes grokking speed is known in another form: frequency-aware sampling that balances token updates accelerates grokking (AlQuabeh et al. 2025, arXiv 2505.15624, abstract checked). Here token frequencies do not explain the gap: in EXP-047 the shuffled arms had exactly the token frequencies of the engineered arms and did not generalize. Literature search: [[paper/lit_grokking_speed_2026-09-27]].
  - *Pre-registered pilot EXP-018 (session 32; control arm prospective):* on a common held-out test set, engineered splits E generalized 2.69 log2 (≈ 6.5×) earlier on average than a control D with the same weight distribution within every anti-diagonal (weights permuted within anti-diagonals; 10/10 seeds, one-sided p = 0.001; time bounded at 8000 steps). D was about as slow as a uniform random split (log2 ratio 0.17, n.s.). In this pilot the speed-up required the engineered pair arrangement that carries the spectral concentration, not only the output marginals. The E and R arms of these seeds had been seen before (EXP-041); the confirmation R5 (n = 20 by its pre-registered power rule) confirmed both contrasts on fresh units (Section 4).
  - *Dose curve with a prediction fixed before the runs (EXP-084, session 32, 10 fresh units, pilot):* We calibrated two phenomenological models on seen runs only. In M_share, time depends on the realized mask target share s through b = T∞ + A/(s − s0). In M_eps, log time is linear in log ε. The two models differed at extreme ε, where s saturates (≈ 0.40–0.43): M_share predicted saturation, M_eps a continued speed-up. The observed median log2(b(ε 32)/b(ε 8)) was −0.11 (M_share −0.14, M_eps −0.82), and ε = 4 fell inside the pre-set band [450, 575], at its lower edge (median 450 steps; M_share predicted 514, M_eps 582). So above ε = 2 the speed-up in this pilot is consistent with following the pair spectrum rather than the extremity of the draw weights. At the low end the model failed: ε = 1 was far slower than predicted (1/10 units within 4000 steps, prediction ≈ 1900) (`lab/experiments/EXP-084-dose-curve/`).
  - *Planting the early signal (EXP-087 pilot and EXP-088, session 39; fresh seeds, rules fixed before any result was read (some additions after the runs had started), no frozen manifest; exploration).* To ask whether the R5 speed-up runs through the early W_E target signal, we added a fixed component on the five target frequencies to the number rows of W_E right after initialization of a uniform random split ("planting": power C × the median initial frequency power per target, random directions from a separate stream; control: an unstructured addition of equal Frobenius norm). In the pilot (10 units, C = 2) planting shortened the bounded time of the random split by 3.42 log2 [3.08, 3.75] (10/10; a lower bound, 3 random-split runs censored at 8000 steps), and the norm control had no effect (−0.09 [−0.33, 0.12]). The planted random split was even faster than the engineered split E2 (−0.63 [−0.99, −0.20]) because the calibration overshot (target share of W_E energy at step 250: 0.40 vs 0.31), so the pre-set mediation reading was "unclear"; across the five arms the share at step 250 ordered the times exactly. EXP-088 (20 fresh units; data arms ε = 2, 4, 8; planting arms C = 1, 2, 4; R descriptive) then placed planted arms on the data dose curve: log2 time linear in the share at step 250, fitted over the three data arms with unit intercepts and a common slope, planted arms counted only inside the share range of their unit's data arms (± 0.03, no further extrapolation). The mean residual of the planted arms was −0.39 log2 (90 % CI [−0.52, −0.27], 95 % CI [−0.55, −0.24], 17/20 units negative), i.e. they generalized ≈ ×1.3 faster than their share predicts; the pre-set equivalence bound ±0.5 log2 (90 % CI) was narrowly missed (reading "unclear"; the same under the registered piecewise-linear sensitivity curve). The direction (planting slightly faster) was known from EXP-087 before EXP-088 was registered. Relative to the full data effect R → E8 (≥ 3.75 log2; R censored at 8000 steps in 3/20 units) the residual is ≈ 10 % or less. *Interpretation (not a claim):* the early target share is consistent with being the main mediator of the speed-up; in this measure the split adds nothing beyond it, and the direct intervention is slightly more effective per unit of share (possibly because it acts from step 0). Planting also steered the final top-5 almost like the data (3.45–3.65 vs 3.65–4.00 of 5 targets, EXP-088). That well-aligned early embeddings speed up grokking is known (Howe 2026b, arXiv 2607.04333; GrokTransfer, arXiv 2504.13292); at most the near-equivalence of a data-driven and a planted early signal on a common dose axis was not found in our search. **Limits:** add 113, one architecture; only C = 2 lies inside the data range (± 0.03) in every unit (C = 1 in 4, C = 4 in 7 units), and the three planting arms of a unit share directions; E4 and E8 are close in share (0.45 / 0.49); the share at 250 is measured after the intervention and so contains the planted part by design (`lab/experiments/EXP-087-planted-signal-mediation/`, `lab/experiments/EXP-088-common-dose-curve/`).
  - *Graded with concentration (post hoc, 4 seeds, session 31):* for seeds 30, 31, 32 and 34, runs sharing initialization, test set and training-set size (3831 pairs), and differing only in the concentration parameter ε of the pair mask (mean target share of M0 0.116 / 0.18 / 0.36 at ε = 1 / 2 / 8), generalized after 425–450 steps at ε = 8, 700–900 steps at ε = 2 and not within 2000 steps at ε = 1, strictly ordered in 4/4 seeds (`lab/experiments/EXP-042-bias-strength/posthoc_speed_dose.py`). Within one level (ε = 2, P1, 50 seeds) the small natural variation of the target share correlated with generalization time across seeds (Spearman −0.58, per-seed means of both arms) but not between the two arms sharing an initialization (the higher-share arm generalized earlier in 28 and later in 29 of 60 such pairs, 3 ties; the 60 pairs include 10 from P1's crossing arm with additional initializations), so this within-level association is unresolved (`lab/confirm/speed_posthoc_share_within.py`).
  - *Other tasks (post hoc, complement test sets):* in the stored EXP-043 runs (GPU, 2000 steps, same initialization per seed) engineered splits (ε = 2) generalized earlier than uniform splits in 10/10 seeds for both multiplication mod 113 and addition mod 97 (sign test p = 0.001 each); the uniform arms never reached the event within 2000 steps, the engineered arms did in 16/20 (multiplication) and 17/20 (addition mod 97) runs (`lab/confirm/speed_posthoc_other_tasks.py`).
- *Early data switches slowed generalization in stored runs; later ones did not (observation, post hoc, session 32; **confirmed on 30 fresh seeds by R6, Appendix C.4**).* The stored switch blocks reused seeds whose frequencies we had already analysed; only their generalization steps were new. The question itself arose in the same session from EXP-020/EXP-041. We bounded the time to the trainer's generalization event at a common 2000 steps from step 0. We compared a switch with training on the destination split alone, using the log2 time ratio (averaged over both directions where both exist). For add 113 the pattern was:
  - A switch after 25 steps generalized later in 28/30 seeds of N28 (mean 0.54 log2, ≈ ×1.45) and in 28/30 seeds of P3 (sign stated before reading the P3 times; mean 0.60 under the common cap).
  - In EXP-056 the median was positive at every overlap level.
  - A switch after 50 steps generalized *earlier* than the destination-only run in 24/30 N28 seeds. The difference between 25 and 50 had mean 0.90 log2 (27/30).
  - These effect sizes are optimistic, because the hypothesis was selected on N28.
  - Zeroing Adam's first moment at 25 reduced the delay (N28: mean 0.54 → 0.41 log2, about a quarter; smaller in 22/30 seeds; still positive in 25/30; `speed_switch_cost_rom_s32.py`, descriptive). On the ten already seen seeds 400–409 (EXP-058; the plain value equals the one read from EXP-056) the delay fell from 0.57 to 0.26 when the first moment was zeroed, to 0.25 when both moments were, and to 0.28 when the whole optimizer was reset. It stayed positive in 8/10 seeds in each case (`speed_switch_optstate_s32.py`). So between about a quarter and just over half of the delay disappeared with the optimizer state. No optimizer reset removed the rest. That the rest sits in the weights is an inference, not a measurement.
  - A possible reason why a switch after the lock-in speeds generalization up: when the new split reaches 99 % training accuracy, test accuracy is already 0.42 (median over runs) after a switch at 50, against 0.16 in the destination-only run at the same step (30/30 seeds). This is consistent with fitting the new split through the already fixed features. At 25 the pre-stated comparison (destination-only at its own memorization step) was also positive (25/30), but under the same-step control, added after the first look, the difference vanished (15/30) (`speed_switch_fitroute_s32.py`).
  - *Open alternative (skeptic review, session 32):* every early change of the training data might cost time, whether or not the frequency sets conflict. The overlap result (more shared pairs, more delay) fits that reading at least as well. A control that switches between two splits with the same target frequencies (EXP-086) decides between the two. *Pilot (session 37; seeds 400–409, known from EXP-056; rule and prediction fixed before the runs):* a switch at t = 25 to a pair-disjoint split A2 with the **same** five targets and matched steering strength did not cost time (C = −0.26 log2, 4/10 seeds positive), whereas the switch to other targets did (+0.57, 8/10); the difference D = +0.82 log2 (9/10 seeds, exact one-sided sign test p = 0.011). A switch between two uniform random splits at t = 25 even sped grokking up (−0.80, 0/10 positive). In first order, A2 pushes against the target directions of A as strongly as B does (gradient cosine −0.52 vs −0.53), so this first-order counter-term does not explain the cost. This favoured a conflict between target sets over a generic early-change cost; the confirmation R8 on 25 fresh seeds holds (D = +0.81 log2 [0.57, 1.04], 24/25; Appendix C.4).
  - More shared pairs between the splits tended to increase the delay (EXP-056 8/10 seeds, p = 0.055, not significant, not monotone in ω; P3 24/30, seen data).
  - Across seeds, how undecided the final choice was (|π(25) − 0.5|) did not predict the delay (ρ = 0.08).
  - Splitting generalization time into memorization time (train accuracy ≥ 0.99 on the current split) and the gap to generalization, the mean delay at 25 lay mostly in the gap: memorization +32 steps, gap +283 of +315 (N28, 47 direction pairs with all events observed; gap delay larger than memorization delay in 37/47; with censored runs counted as lower bounds, the gap carried 92 % of the mean delay over all 60 pairs, gap delay larger in 49/60). At 50 (57 pairs), memorization of the new split took longer (+92) but the gap shortened (−237) (`speed_switch_decompose_s32.py`).
  - In N29 (20 further seeds, switch arms only) the switch at 25 generalized later than the one at 50 in 20/20 seeds (mean 1.01 log2).
  - With re-initialization at a switch at 50, attention resets delayed generalization slightly more than MLP resets (N29b, 15/20, mean +0.15 log2). Value-path resets delayed it clearly more than equally sized query/key resets (N29c, 19/20, +1.31 log2). This is the same ordering in which they reduce persistence (K4d, K4e). We cannot tell whether this reflects an undone lock-in or simply more destroyed function (`speed_switch_resets_s32.py`). Immediate damage does not explain it. Relative to the plain switch, every reset *lowered* the training loss on the new split right after the switch (MLP −0.71, attention −0.68, value path −0.61, query/key −0.23 at step 50). The value-path reset lowered it more than the query/key reset in 20/20 seeds, yet generalized slowest (`speed_reset_damage_s32.py`, descriptive).
  - On a finer grid (seeds 400–409, EXP-059 with EXP-056, same splits and initialization) the mean delay was 0.27, 0.38, 0.53, 0.57, 0.55, 0.33 and −0.67 log2 at t = 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35 and 50. Predictions were stated before reading the EXP-059 switch times; the destination-only baselines and the switch at 25 (EXP-056) had been read before. The delay rose, peaked at 25 (on fresh seeds R6 peaked at t = 20, Appendix C.4) and changed sign between 35 and 50, where π rose from 0.56 to 1.05 (`speed_switch_curve_s32.py`).
The window is not fixed at 25–50:
  - In EXP-020 (CPU, 5 seeds, ≈ 73 % shared pairs) a switch at 50 was still slow, and one at 150 was not slower than the destination alone.
  - In EXP-044 (one direction, 10 seeds each, frequencies seen before) a delay at 25 also appeared for addition mod 97 (6/6 non-tied seeds, p = 0.016; heavily censored: 4 seeds tied at the cap, only 1/10 switch runs generalized within 2000 steps) and, not significantly, for multiplication mod 113 (7/10, p = 0.17). The pre-stated contrast C(25) > C(50) was not met (add 97 4/4 non-tied, p = 0.06; mul 113 4/10). The delay persisted at 50 (mean +0.29 and +0.44 log2; 5 vs 2 and 7 vs 3 seeds). A switch at 150 was faster than the destination alone in 10/10 seeds of both tasks (`speed_switch_cost_tasks_s32.py`).
  - Descriptively, the delay vanished in those conditions where the persistence π(t) had reached about 1 or more (N28 at 50: 1.0; EXP-044 at 150: 1.15–1.24) and remained where π(t) ≤ 0.86. This is a condition-level association, not a per-seed one.
The comparison replaces the first t destination updates by origin updates, so it mixes an interruption of the lock-in with less destination exposure and more distinct pairs. Less exposure alone would predict a larger delay at 50 than at 25, the opposite of N28 (`lab/confirm/speed_switch_cost_*_s32.py`, [[confirm/R6_REGISTRATION_DRAFT|R6]]).
- *What sets the lock-in clock: Adam's first-moment window (EXP-081, EXP-089, EXP-090, EXP-091; session 40; fresh seeds except EXP-091, rules and code fixed before the runs, the trainer changes and the EXP-089 result checked by an independent read-only agent, no frozen manifest; exploration; the main contrasts of EXP-090 and EXP-091 were later confirmed on fresh seeds in R9, Appendix D.2).* All three use the N28/EXP-059 protocol (add 113, pair-disjoint ω = 0 split pairs, switch A → B and B → A at t, then 2000 steps (EXP-089/090/091: default learning rate and betas after the switch; EXP-081: the cell's betas throughout); π = persistence of the old choice in the log energy ratio, against pure runs of the same seed and, in EXP-081, of the same β cell). **Fixed Λ, more steps (EXP-089, 10 seeds):** with the learning rate scaled by 0.25 for 100 steps (Λ = 25, as 25 default steps), π was higher than after 25 default steps, +0.24 [0.17, 0.34] (95 % bootstrap CI; 10/10 seeds), about as high as after 33 default steps. The difference was already present in W_E at the switch. So the Appendix D.1 shortfall from a pure Λ clock reappears on fresh seeds with a different measure. **Equal windows in Λ (EXP-090, 16 seeds):** Adam averages over a fixed number of *steps* (≈ 10 for β₁ = 0.9), so at lr × 0.25 its windows are four times shorter in Λ. Rescaling the betas only before the switch so that the windows are equal in Λ (1 − β′ = c(1 − β), i.e. β′ = 0.975/0.995; bias-corrected moments kept continuous at the switch) removed the difference: π(lr × 0.25, 100 steps, β′) − π(25 default steps) = +0.002 [−0.024, 0.024], while the replication without rescaling gave +0.16 [0.09, 0.24] and the paired contrast between the two 100-step arms was +0.16 [0.10, 0.23] (15/16). Rescaling β₁ alone was enough (−0.02 relative to 25 default steps, slightly below). A caveat for the comparisons with the 25-step arm (not for the paired contrast between the two 100-step arms): after the switch Adam's step counter stands at 100 instead of 25; the separation of the two frequency sets in W_E at the switch, which does not depend on it, gives the same reading (ratio 0.04 of the unrescaled gap). **Larger learning rate (EXP-091, the EXP-089 seeds, 10 seeds, pilot):** at lr × 2 for 15 steps (Λ = 30) the default windows are twice as long in Λ; rescaling the betas to 0.8/0.96 raised π by +0.05 [0.02, 0.08] (10/10), from about 27 to about 29 equivalent default steps (Λ = 30 would give 30; from cell means, coarse). **Varying β₁ at the standard learning rate (EXP-081, 10 seeds):** zeroing Adam's first moment at t = 25 lowered π by 0.08 / 0.14 / 0.19 for β₁ = 0.8 / 0.9 / 0.95 (contrast 0.95 vs 0.8 positive in 9/10 seeds, sign test p = 0.011), of the same order and trend as the momentum tail of a scalar Adam model (estimated 2.7 / 8.0 / 17.4 against predicted 4.0–4.5 / 8.7–10.8 / 16–24 update equivalents; two of three below the predicted range). The lock-in window did not scale with the β₂ horizon (β₂ = 0.95 or 0.995 changed π at t = 33 by −0.05 and +0.01; a 1/(1 − β₂) scaling would have predicted about +0.5 and −0.5). Post hoc, the lock-in present at the switch without the tail fell with β₁ (π after zeroing 0.34 / 0.21 / 0.13; ordered in 9/10 seeds). *Interpretation (not a claim):* in these pilots (one Λ per learning-rate factor, c = 0.25 and 2) the early lock-in follows summed learning rate once Adam's first-moment lag is also measured in summed learning rate; a longer lag makes the early motion less frequency-selective, and the lag's tail after a switch adds to persistence. The β rescaling (1 − β ∝ learning rate) is the deterministic continuous-time matching (cf. Barakat & Bianchi, arXiv 1810.02263); it has the same form as, but is not, Malladi et al.'s SDE square-root rule (2022, arXiv 2205.10287: batch × κ, learning rate × √κ, 1 − β → κ(1 − β), i.e. 1 − β ∝ (learning rate)²; corrected in session 41, earlier text said "matches"); its consequence for lock-in was not found in our search. **Limits:** pilots with 10–16 seeds each, one task and architecture, full batch, one Λ and one learning-rate factor per experiment (EXP-091 on seeds already used in EXP-089); the window matching is first order; the post hoc β₁ ordering in EXP-081 was examined after a reviewer's hint from EXP-089 (`lab/experiments/EXP-081-optimizer-clock/`, `EXP-089-lambda-fixed-steps/`, `EXP-090-beta-window-lambda/`, `EXP-091-beta-window-c2/`).
- Further pilots: steering also in a shared-embedding MLP, at 4× width and for non-modular integer addition (EXP-045, 049, 048) — confirmed on fresh seeds by P4 (Appendix A.2).
- *How a shorter momentum lag strengthens lock-in (post hoc on the stored R9 runs, session 41; measures not read before, exploration).* (i) **Composition, not amount:** at equal Λ, the W_E displacement W_E(t) − W_E(0) under the shorter lag (c = 0.25, default betas) had a higher share of its group power on the first split's targets than with rescaled betas (log ratio +0.128 [0.122, 0.134], 36/36 seeds) and a smaller increase in norm (+0.089); at c = 2 the rescaled (shorter-lag) arm likewise +0.056 in share and +0.031 in norm. More time does the opposite: from t = 25 to t = 30 default steps the share rose by +0.051 and the norm by +0.175 (all values in (i) are mean log ratios). So a shorter lag is not equivalent to more time: relative to more time it changes the composition of the early motion more than its size (log f / log N 1.4 and 1.8 against 0.29 for more time), although the norm also rises. (ii) **Premise:** in the 72 pure R9 runs the increment's share on the own targets rose from 0.21 (steps 0→50) to 0.46 (50→250) (72/72; chance 5/56 ≈ 0.09), i.e. the early W_E motion (Adam updates plus decay, not the raw gradient) becomes more target-selective (coarse: no snapshots inside the first 25 steps; not causal), consistent with a longer window at the switch still averaging in older, less selective updates. In EXP-092 the cumulative selectivity at the switch likewise rose with t (0.173 / 0.183 / 0.193 at t = 20 / 25 / 30). (iii) **State at the switch:** across the six R9 arms, mean π lies almost on one line in the separation of the two target sets in W_E at the switch (R² 0.97 over arm means; 0.60 within seeds); both are W_E energy measures, so this is a hint that the history acts through the state at the switch, not a test. *Reading (not a claim):* momentum acts as a low-pass filter over a gradient whose target selectivity grows during the first steps (`lab/confirm/R9_displacement_s41.py`, `R9_increment_selectivity_s41.py`).
- *A momentum-lag clock predicts unseen cells, except for few very large steps (EXP-092; 16 fresh seeds, predictions and readings fixed before the runs; exploration).* Model: the direction of motion lags by the mean age of Adam's bias-corrected first moment, so lock-in should follow Λ_eff = c·t − c·lag(β₁, t), with lag(β, t) = Σ k βᵏ / Σ βᵏ over k = 0 … t − 1 (post hoc on the six R9 arm means: RMSE 0.027 against 0.060 for Λ and 0.059 for steps). Calibrated on the experiment's own t = 25 and t = 30 default cells, it predicted five new cells (t = 20; β₁ = 0.8 or 0.95 before the switch only, at default learning rate and Λ = 25; c = 0.5 with t = 50; c = 4 with t = 6, Λ = 24) with a mean absolute error of 0.029 (about 0.009 without the c = 4 cell), against 0.067 for a Λ clock and 0.149 for a step clock (bootstrap CIs of both differences above 0; registered reading "lag clock supported"). Changing β₁ only before the switch shifted π at equal Λ in the predicted direction (π(β₁ = 0.8) − π(default) = +0.083 [0.046, 0.123], 14/16; π(default) − π(β₁ = 0.95) = +0.037 [0.016, 0.061], 13/16), which neither a Λ nor a step clock predicts. Four cells lay within 0.015 of the prediction in their means (per-seed intervals up to about ±0.03); **c = 4 with t = 6 fell far below it** (−0.107 [−0.16, −0.06], post hoc residual), and its early motion was larger than at t = 20 but the least target-selective of all cells. Candidate explanations (not tested): Adam's first, nearly sign-like steps, whose share of Λ grows with c, or overshooting. **Limits:** pilot, one task, π is an energy measure, linear calibration extrapolated to some cells, first-order lag measure (`lab/experiments/EXP-092-momentum-lag-clock/`). *Range (EXP-093, 16 other fresh seeds, registered before the runs):* at fixed Λ = 24 with c = 2, 3, 4, 6, 8 (t = 12 … 3), the lag clock predicted nearly equal π, but π fell from 0.27 to 0.09, below the prediction in every cell and increasingly with c (−0.04 [−0.07, −0.00] at c = 2 to −0.25 [−0.31, −0.18] at c = 8; registered reading "mixed": no cell within ±0.03); c = 4 replicated (−0.13). The size of the early displacement was nearly the same in all cells, its target share fell with c. An added Euler delay of c/2 per step, fixed before the results, explained only part (mean absolute error 0.093 against 0.138). So the lag clock describes lock-in only for learning-rate factors up to about 1 in this setting; with fewer, larger steps at equal Λ the early motion is less target-selective and lock-in weaker (`lab/experiments/EXP-093-lag-clock-range/`). Post hoc, across the 15 cell means of EXP-092 and EXP-093, π was nearly linear in the target share of the early displacement at the switch (R² 0.93; adding its norm: 0.94; norm alone: 0.56), including the cells where the lag clock failed; both are W_E energy measures on the same target sets, so this is a hint, not a test. *Windows vs. step count (EXP-094, 16 further fresh seeds, registered):* with Adam's windows also matched in Λ (β′ = 1 − c(1 − β)) at Λ = 24, a shortfall against 24 default steps remained and grew with c (c = 2: 0.03 [0.015, 0.053]; c = 4: 0.05 [0.023, 0.079]; c = 8: 0.17 [0.13, 0.22]; registered reading "partial"); at c = 4 matching recovered about half of the gap (+0.049 [0.019, 0.082], 12/16). So the step-fixed windows explain part of the large-step deficit, and a second part, growing with c, remains (`lab/experiments/EXP-094-evaluations-vs-window/`). *Gradient evaluations vs. Adam step (EXP-095, 16 further fresh seeds, registered; trainer option `--pre-switch-grad-every k`):* keeping the 24 default Adam steps (learning rate, betas, weight decay unchanged) but computing a fresh gradient before the switch only every k steps, and reusing the stored one in between, reproduced the large-step deficit: with 3 evaluations (k = 8) the shortfall against 24 evaluations was +0.141 [0.060, 0.211] (13/16), indistinguishable from 3 large steps with matched windows (+0.141 [0.084, 0.194], a replication; EXP-094: 0.17; difference between the two +0.000 [−0.036, 0.035]; registered reading "evaluations count"). With 6 evaluations (k = 4) it was small (+0.020 [−0.008, 0.050]); with the initial gradient only (k = 24) it was +0.187 [0.111, 0.266], and W_E moved further (displacement norm 2.87 against 2.36) but with a lower target share (0.142 against 0.180; π 0.097 against 0.284). So in this setting, lock-in up to Λ = 24 depends on re-evaluating the gradient along the path (or on avoiding near-sign steps with a frozen gradient; not separated, Appendix D.3) (whether through self-reinforcement of the target components or through correction of the stale initial direction is not tested). The initial gradient alone under Adam (a sign-descent version of, not the same as, the object of the first-order account in Appendix G, which makes no claim about lock-in, Appendix G iv; see the limits below) gives only weak lock-in, with a lower target share as in the sign-descent simulation of Appendix G (i). The remaining large-step deficit of EXP-094 is accounted for by the number of gradient evaluations; the coarse Adam step (8× learning rate, β′) adds nothing measurable on top (with the step-counter caveat below). *(Session 46: on 48 fresh seeds this equivalence was not confirmed, R10 H2, Appendix D.3: r₈ = +0.057 [0.038, 0.078]; this sentence and the preceding one on the remaining large-step deficit hold only for the pilot.)* The post hoc line π(f) underpredicted all three reused-gradient cells (mean absolute error over all five cells 0.062), so the target share is not a complete state variable. **Limits:** pilot, one task; the equality of k = 8 and the three large steps compares cells whose Adam step counter differs after the switch (3 vs 24, so the first new gradient enters m̂ with weight 0.29 vs 0.11), so it may partly be a cancellation; number and spacing of evaluations are confounded at fixed Λ, and with a frozen gradient Adam's bias-corrected moments are exactly m̂ = g₀ and v̂ = g₀², so every step is lr·g₀/(|g₀| + ε) ≈ lr·sign(g₀) per entry, plus decoupled weight decay (99.9 % of the W_E entries of the k = 24 displacement within 10 % of a full sign step, measured post hoc): k = 24 is approximately sign descent along the initial gradient (Adam's direction is the gradient sign and its step shrinks with the gradient's relative variance, which is zero for a frozen gradient; Balles & Hennig, 2018), not first order under gradient flow. Post hoc, on the displacement corrected for the weight-decay shrinkage of W_E(0) (target shares 0.182 and 0.143 instead of 0.180 and 0.142 above), binarising the displacement of the default arm lowered its target share from 0.182 to 0.160, i.e. by 56 % [53, 59] of the gap to k = 24. The displacements of k = 8 (45 % of entries full sign steps) and of the three large steps (33 %) were less quantised than the default (54 %), so this concerns mainly k = 24; the comparison of k = 8 with the large steps is not directly affected, but this is not tested. So roughly half of the target-share gap with the initial gradient alone may reflect this sign quantisation rather than staleness; nothing is shown about the π deficit itself (seen data; the binarised default displacement is only a surrogate for sign(g₀); a separating test with linear normalised steps is prepared, EXP-097) (`lab/experiments/EXP-095-gradient-feedback/`, `posthoc_sign_s43.py`).

## Appendix G: First-order theory

Under near-uniform initial outputs, the first gradient on embedding row t is a sum over the training pairs containing t, mapped through the initial Jacobian; under isotropic Jacobians its expected Fourier power at k is
proportional to the coherent mask spectrum M0c minus a marginal term for the transformer (shared path for both positions) and to M0 minus marginal terms for the MLP (independent halves). The output-uniform part of a row's own target vector cancels exactly (the row's pair count still scales its gradient); the other operand's token frequencies do not (corrected in session 25, see 5.2), so the prediction for a frequency-matched
control with shuffled pairs (no steering) rests on the near-uniform marginals of the engineered splits, whose spectrum is nevertheless target-enriched (5.2); this is consistent with pilot EXP-047, not a confirmation. Derivation and its limits: [[BEFUND-split-mechanismus]].

**5.1 Setting (draft text, session 25; post hoc explanation, not an independent test).** Let m(a, b) ∈ {0, 1} mark the training pairs, N = Σ m, and c = a + b mod p. At
initialization the logits are small, so the softmax output is close to uniform, s ≈ 𝟙/p, and the cross-entropy gradient with respect to the logits of pair (a, b) is
s − e_c ≈ −P⊥ e_c with P⊥ = I − 𝟙𝟙ᵀ/p. Write J_L, J_R for the Jacobians of the logits with respect to the embedding of the left and right operand, assumed at first order to be
the same for all pairs. The gradient on embedding row t is then

g_t ≈ −(1/N) [ J_Lᵀ P⊥ ℓ_t + J_Rᵀ P⊥ r_t ],  ℓ_t(c) = m(t, c − t),  r_t(c) = m(c − t, t).

**5.2 Frequency content.** Taking the DFT over the token index t (ℓ̂_k(c) = Σ_t ℓ_t(c) ω^{−kt}, ω = e^{2πi/p}) and assuming isotropic random Jacobians at initialization,

- *shared path* (transformer: at initialization the nearly uniform attention mixes both positions into the same value/output path, J_L ≈ J_R; neglecting the attention-score derivative and the pair dependence of the MLP gating at initialization):
  E‖ĝ_k‖² ∝ ‖P⊥(ℓ̂_k + r̂_k)‖² = Σ_c |ℓ̂_k(c) + r̂_k(c)|² − |n̂_L(k) + n̂_R(k)|²/p, the *coherent mask spectrum* M0c minus a marginal term;
- *separate paths* (shared-embedding MLP: a and b enter different halves of W_in, J_L and J_R independent): the cross term averages out,
  E‖ĝ_k‖² ∝ ‖P⊥ℓ̂_k‖² + ‖P⊥r̂_k‖², the *mask spectrum* M0 minus marginal terms.

Here n̂_L(k) = Σ_c ℓ̂_k(c) is the DFT of how often each token occurs as a left operand (likewise n̂_R). The subtracted term is the power (p·|mean|²) of the c-mean component of ℓ̂_k(c) + r̂_k(c): P⊥ removes
every component that does not vary along the output c. What cancels exactly is therefore the output-uniform part of a row's *own* target vector (its n_t u term); the row's pair count still scales its gradient (‖P⊥ℓ_t‖² = n_t(1 − n_t/p) for 0/1 entries). Token frequencies still enter through the
*other* operand: for m(a, b) = ρ(a), ℓ̂_k(c) = ρ̂(k) is constant in c and vanishes, but r̂_k(c) = ω^{−kc} ρ̂(k)* is not, and the shared-path power is p |ρ̂(k)|² (checked numerically,
session 25). **Prediction 1 (quantitative, not "marginals never steer"):** a control that keeps the a/b token frequencies of an engineered split but shuffles its pairs keeps only the
marginal contribution (plus random pair noise); for the EXP-016 construction the marginals are no more unequal than in a random split (coefficient of variation 0.14), although their spectrum is target-enriched
(mean target rank 11.6 vs 27.5 by chance); after centring, the first-order spectrum of the shuffled splits is at chance (shared path, recomputed in session 25: mean 0-based target rank
26.2 vs 27.5, share 0.090 vs 0.191 for the engineered splits), so such a control is predicted to steer at most weakly. A split with strongly structured token frequencies would be predicted to steer towards the frequencies of ρ.
**Prediction 2 (architecture contrast):** the first gradient of the transformer should follow M0c, that of the shared-embedding MLP M0.

**5.3 Status of the predictions (all exploratory, known seeds).** Prediction 2 matches the measured first gradients (Spearman ρ 0.77 for M0c vs 0.57 for M0 in the transformer; 0.24 vs 0.37 in
the MLP, 9/10 seeds), measured before the derivation was written, so it is an explanation rather than a test. The expected outcome for pilot EXP-047 (no steering by the shuffled control) was noted before its runs, but derived
from the uncorrected argument that all token frequencies cancel; the corrected quantitative form (Appendix G) was written after the result. A control with exactly matched a/b token frequencies
but random pair structure showed no detectable steering (Δ̄ 0.3 on the top-5 overlap score, p = 0.33), while the pair structure did (D̄ 6.8, 10/10 seeds, p = 0.001); a pilot on 10 seeds,
not a confirmation. For the *final* frequencies of the transformer, the registered check EXP-019 (rule fixed before the runs; 12 units: EXP-018 random-split arm, GPU, plus two CPU baselines) found M0c better than M0 (r̄ 0.232 vs 0.315, mean paired difference 0.082, one-sided sign-flip p = 0.0012; secondary random-split arm D, n = 10: p = 0.004); adding the initial W_E energy improved the prediction further (descriptive, p = 0.022). For the *final* frequencies of the MLP, M0 is only descriptively better than M0c (r̄ 0.323 vs 0.351, lower is better; 6/10 seeds, p ≈ 0.21). The order *within* the target set, by contrast, does not follow the prediction (session 28, pilot EXP-045, 10 seeds, `lab/confirm/EXP045_posthoc_within.py`): at step 2000 the MLP's target order follows M0c (mean within-arm ρ 0.60) more than M0 (0.46; the predicted M0 > M0c holds in 3/10 seeds, one-sided p 0.92), and by step 10 000 both have faded (0.17 / 0.20). Prediction 2 therefore holds for the first gradient but not for the later order within the target set; M0c predicting the fine order (C1) is not specific evidence for the shared-path derivation.

**5.4 Limits of the first-order argument.** (i) It describes the gradient at initialization. With AdamW the first update is approximately lr · sign(g) coordinate-wise (bias-corrected
moments give m̂/√v̂ = g/|g| at step 1). This sign-like update, to which the decoupled weight-decay term −lr·λ·W_E(0) adds the initialization spectrum, keeps the dominant frequencies but can spread some power to other frequencies; the spectrum of the *update* is therefore not exactly the one derived above. In a simulation of the first-order model (isotropic random Jacobian, d = 128, P1 construction on 10 calibration
seeds × 2 arms, session 25, numpy only) the coordinate-wise sign of the gradient kept all five targets in its top five in every case (target share of the power 0.152 vs 0.191 for
the gradient itself); this checks only the model, not the network. In a
two-hot quadratic pilot network with an activation switch (EXP-033, exploratory), replacing AdamW by plain gradient descent in the first phase only (to matched amplitude; the second phase
was always AdamW; one stage tested) still gave a persistent bias towards the split's targets, slightly stronger (ratio 1.26 [1.10, 1.46]); sign-GD reproduced AdamW. Whether this holds for
the transformer is untested. (ii) It describes the initial gradient (and, approximately, the first sign-like Adam updates), i.e. which frequencies the network starts to grow, not which survive: in the engineered splits some early-weak
targets were displaced by step 2000 by second harmonics fold(2k) of targets of the same arm (EXP-016, post hoc, 14/14 in seeds 10–15; the registered check EXP-021, whose rule was fixed before its 18 runs existed but whose data were partly seen descriptively, found 22 of 23 non-target top-5 members to be fold(2k) of the arm's own targets, expected 2.2, Poisson-binomial p = 7e-22, and 0/23 for the other arm's targets; session 36). In the MLP pilot EXP-045 the W_E top-5 contained no non-target member in any of 20 runs, so the question whether even harmonics are transformer-specific (He et al. 2026a report only odd harmonics in the input weights of a two-layer ReLU network) cannot be answered from the top-5 (N45, exploration). (iii) The isotropy assumption on the Jacobians is not checked beyond the first-gradient
correlations. (iv) It says nothing about why the early choice persists after a data switch (K4); the lab's amplitude model for that (H40) was tested by EXP-040 and not supported (pre-registered pilot, 4 known seeds; registered reading "unclear", no seed shifted in the predicted direction); the lock-in clock is treated empirically in Appendix F, Appendix D.1, Appendix D.2, Appendix D.3 and Appendix D.4 (EXP-081/089–095, R3, R9, R10, R11); the first-order account makes no prediction about it.
The derivation in the simplest alternating-gradient-flow model (AGF) does *not* reduce to M0 (EXP-076, negative), so the link to AGF-type theories remains open.

## Appendix H: Reproduction from scratch

Every confirmed number can be regenerated from its frozen block; the main-text claims listed below can also be rebuilt from scratch. (i) From the frozen blocks: job list, bound runs and frozen analysis per block (`lab/confirm/<BLOCK>_jobs.txt`, `lab/tools/confirm_<block>.py --analyze lab/confirm/<BLOCK>_manifest.json`, run at the manifest's commit; code hashes are checked against the manifest; reanalysis blocks C1–C4: `lab/confirm/C*_analyze.py lab/confirm/C*_manifest.json`). (ii) From scratch: one script per claim in `lab/paper/repro/` rebuilds the splits from the registered construction, trains with a lean trainer (`train.py`: the lab trainer's standard path, optionally with i.i.d. minibatches drawn from the lab trainer's own order stream (same salt and seed, a new permutation per epoch) and with its dense accuracy trace (evaluation only)), evaluates with the frozen statistics and compares with the frozen summary. The acceptance rule was fixed before the first equivalence check: if `train.py` matches stored runs within a relative 10⁻⁴ at all common steps (it matched bit for bit: in full batch, and at batch 256 and 64 over 2 500 steps of one seed), every script's tolerance, each fixed before its full run, applies unchanged and a miss counts as "not reproduced". All full runs on one AMD RX 7900 XT (ROCm 7.2.1, PyTorch 2.9.1, Windows 11).
