## Appendix I: Minibatch training and the lock-in clock in detail

**Question.** All results above use full-batch training. LeDoux (2026) found, under minibatch training with a fixed, structured example order, the same fundamental frequency across random training subsets. We ask whether the steering by the set survives minibatch training, and what happens when an order favours a different frequency than the set.

**Design (pilot EXP-100; the confirmation follows as its own registration).** Addition mod 113, the setup of Section 2. Per seed, engineered splits F and G whose five targets exclude the frequencies favoured by the order, and a uniform random split R. Arms: full batch for 2000 and for 30 000 steps (a budget-matched reference); i.i.d. minibatches of 256 and of 64 pairs (AdamW); SGD with momentum 0.9 (batch 256; learning rate calibrated beforehand on separate runs); and a fixed stride order after LeDoux, pairs sorted by (a mod ⌊√p⌋, a) = (a mod 10, a), identical in every epoch (batch 256). The stride order puts its spectral weight on frequency 11 (49 %), then 23, 34, 12, 45 and 22 (O); the sets carry no more weight on O than chance. The random split with i.i.d. and with stride order measures the order effect alone. A feasibility step before the pilot tests whether the stride order acts at all at 30 % data, at batch 256, 64 and 16; if it acts only at a smaller batch, the conflict arm is also run there (with i.i.d. and stride arms at that batch size), and if it acts at neither, the conflict is reported as not testable at 30 % data, as fixed before the runs. Rationale, computed before any run from the split files (first order: no optimizer, no weight decay; at most a necessary condition): under full-batch training the frequency choice starts to persist within the first 25–50 steps (Result 3), and summed over whole epochs the stride batches reproduce the set. On the random split (mean over 8 seeds), the excess order-frequency share of the summed batch masks over i.i.d. batches is 0.005 after 50 steps at batch 256 (15 steps per epoch); at batch 64 (60 steps per epoch) it is 0.147 after 25 steps, 0.047 after 50 steps and 0 after one full epoch. The value at 50 steps lies at the edge of our criterion, half of the engineered split's target excess (0.5 × 0.094 = 0.047; 2 of 8 seeds fall below it), so whether the order can compete within the lock-in window at batch 64 is open and is decided empirically. LeDoux's order effect was strong at ≈ 1165 steps per epoch (only the stride order generalized) and modest at about 10 steps per epoch (p = 97, 26.5 % data; fixed orders ≈ 20 % faster); our regime at batch 256 lies on the modest side. At batch 16 (240 steps per epoch) the same first-order computation gives an order excess of 0.194 after 50 steps, twice the set's target excess, and only 0.21 epochs fit into the lock-in window, so even i.i.d. batches carry less of the set's spectrum early on (early target share 0.10 against 0.18 at batch 256); batch 16 was added to the feasibility step for this reason, before any run.

**Readings (fixed before the runs).** Steering under minibatch: Δ_pow (as in Section 3) with confidence intervals per arm, also at equal step count (2000). Conflict: "set wins", "order wins" or "both act", judged only if the order is shown to act (otherwise "not testable"); measured by Δ_pow under the stride order, the order frequencies' share of the embedding energy, and the peak frequency. Speed: time to generalization in steps and epochs, engineered against random split.

**Result (pilot EXP-100, 8 seeds, exploration; all numbers independently recomputed).** With i.i.d. minibatches of 256 and of 64 pairs, the engineered splits still steer the learned frequencies (Δ_pow 9.60 [8.98, 10.21] and 9.85 [9.00, 10.73] at the end of 30 000 steps, against 10.28 [9.24, 11.21] for full batch with the same budget); the steering of Result 1 is not a full-batch artefact in this setting. As predicted by the first-order dilution estimate (which assumed the full-batch window; see below), it is weaker at batch 64 at equal step count (at step 2000: full batch 8.36, batch 256 8.05, batch 64 7.29); at the end of the budget this difference is gone. At 30 % data a fixed stride order did not shift the learned frequencies at either batch size (peak frequency in O in 0/16 runs at each; order-share difference on the engineered splits +0.004 [−0.003, 0.015] and +0.005 [−0.000, 0.011]), as a first-order estimate predicted for batch 256 (hypothesis: an epoch of 15 steps is shorter than the lock-in window); for batch 64 it predicted an edge case, and the feasibility runs showed an order effect there only through one seed (+0.05), the pilot none; the order effect reported by LeDoux (2026) at 0.3 % data (an epoch of ≈ 1165 steps) does not appear in this regime. On a random split the evidence for an order effect is intermediate (peak in O in 0/8 and 1/8 stride runs, but an order-share difference whose CI lies below 0, driven by i.i.d. runs (4 of 8 seeds at batch 256, order share up to 0.57) whose random split itself favours O); we report it as unclear. SGD with momentum could not be calibrated (no learning rate generalized in both calibration seeds) and is not evaluable. Engineered splits generalized ≈ 4.3× faster than random splits also under minibatches at batch 256 (median 77 against 333 epochs; pilot only, descriptive, not part of the confirmation). **Limits:** pilot seeds; at batch 64 many runs were not settled at the end (final train accuracy below 0.99 in 7/16 i.i.d. and 14/16 stride runs), so its end values are read partly from unstable networks. At batch 16 (240 steps per epoch) the network did not generalize with the default weight decay 1 within 30 000 steps (3 feasibility seeds, random split; test accuracy ≤ 0.73); with weight decay 0.1 it learns, and the order-against-set test in this long-epoch regime (EXP-106) and the confirmation on fresh seeds are reported below. **The lock-in window under minibatch (pilot, 8 seeds, switch at 25 or 50 steps, both directions).** The full-batch reference replicated on these seeds (π(25) = 0.38, π(50) = 0.87; difference +0.49 [0.39, 0.59]). Under i.i.d. minibatches of 256, the early lock-in of Result 3 did not appear by 50 steps: the choice does not yet persist after 50 steps (π(25) = −0.01, π(50) = −0.02; difference −0.00 [−0.05, 0.05]). Post hoc, at an equal horizon (step 2000) π was also ≈ 0, so this is not an effect of the longer training after the switch. At batch 256, 50 steps are 3.3 epochs, against 50 epochs in full batch; a follow-up (EXP-107, same 8 pilot seeds, switch at 100–1500 steps, exploration) found the window later in steps and earlier in epochs: π(100) = 0.33 [0.24, 0.42], π(200) = 0.85 [0.78, 0.92], π ≈ 1.00 from 375 steps (25 epochs) on; the half-point lies near 133 steps (8.9 epochs) against about 31 steps (31 epochs) in full batch (linear interpolation; π read at step 5000 here and at step 2000 in the reference; energy measure; one batch size; independently recomputed). So a lock-in (energy measure) also appears under minibatches of 256, but it follows neither a pure step nor a pure epoch clock. A batch series on the same 8 seeds, with predictions fixed before the runs (EXP-108; exploration; independently recomputed; its mean half-point at batch 256 is 127 steps, averaged per seed, against ≈ 133 read off the mean π above), placed the half-point at about 62 steps for batch 1024 (predicted 60–67 by a square-root clock anchored at full batch or at batch 256) and 290 for batch 64 (predicted 240–266; later than predicted): the number of steps to lock-in grew roughly as (N/B)^α with α = 0.54 [0.52, 0.56] (0.556 [0.513, 0.595] without the full-batch point), i.e. with the square root of the steps per epoch. One simple reading, derived in this project (AI-assisted, see the AI use disclosure) from the sign-like updates of Adam (Li et al., 2024, whose sign model gives an expected update ∝ √B·μ/σ while √B·μ/σ is small; cf. the Adam SDE of Malladi et al., 2022), is that lock-in occurs once the data-driven drift has covered a fixed distance; it predicts t½ ∝ 1/(lr·√B). At double learning rate (EXP-109, 2 of the seeds, pilot, not independently recomputed) the half-point halved at batch 1024 (≈ 31 steps) but shrank only by ≈ ×0.75 at batch 64, so this reading is at best partial. **Confirmation (N54b, frozen before any run, 10 fresh seeds, batch 1024/256/64 at learning rates 10⁻³ and 2·10⁻³, 840 runs; independently recomputed).** At lr 10⁻³ the mean slope of log t½ against log(N/B) was α = 0.583 [0.560, 0.606] (registered square-root band [0.3, 0.7]; Holm-p 5·10⁻⁶), with half-points of 58, 114 and 289 steps. Doubling the learning rate raised the slope in every seed (Δα = +0.139 [0.098, 0.178], 10/10, Holm-p 6·10⁻⁵): it shortened lock-in to 0.58 [0.54, 0.62] of its duration at batch 1024 but only to 0.85 [0.78, 0.92] at batch 64. So the square-root clock replicates on fresh seeds at the default learning rate, and the simplest sign-drift model (t½ ∝ 1/(lr·√B)) does not suffice, mainly at small batches (Δα between batch 256 and 64: +0.21 [0.13, 0.29]; between 1024 and 256: +0.07 [−0.01, 0.14]); log t½ is curved (two-point slopes 0.48 and 0.68 at lr 10⁻³), so α is an average slope over N/B = 3.7–60, not a clean power law; with N fixed, steps per epoch and batch size are not separated. In a model comparison fixed before the N54b results (exploration), t½ ≈ 23.6·√(N/B)/λ + 2.2·(N/B) (λ = lr/10⁻³; a drift term plus about two epochs) fitted the six cell means better than a free power law. In our search (29 September 2026) we did not find a prior measurement of a square-root batch-size scaling of an early lock-in time at fixed learning rate.

**Confirmation (L0, frozen before any run, 10 fresh seeds, independently recomputed).** The steering under i.i.d. minibatches was confirmed at batch 256 (Δ_pow = 9.43 [9.06, 9.81], 10/10 seeds, Holm-p 4·10⁻¹²) and at batch 64 (9.60 [8.79, 10.46], 10/10, Holm-p 3·10⁻⁹). At batch 64, 12 of 20 runs had not settled at the end of the budget (final train accuracy below 0.99; descriptive, post hoc as announced; H2 therefore claims steering at the end of the budget, not in converged networks). Data order and the lock-in window were not part of this confirmation (the lock-in window under minibatches is confirmed separately in N54b, above). **Long epochs (EXP-106, pilot, 8 seeds, batch 16, weight decay 0.1).** Steering held (Δ_pow = 9.21 [8.82, 9.60]); by the pre-set rule the conflict was not testable (no shift on the engineered splits, order-share difference [−0.005, 0.012]; order-alone reading 'unclear', peak in O in 3/8 random-split runs). Descriptively, on random splits the order raised the order share by +0.16 [0.07, 0.24] (+0.14 without the three seeds seen in the probe; about 0 in the three seeds whose i.i.d. run already carried 0.20–0.24 on O), and on the engineered splits it delayed generalization by 0.67 log2 [0.42, 0.93] (≈ ×1.6, 15/16 pairs; no delay on random splits). In this pilot the order thus shifted the spectrum on random splits but not on engineered splits, where it only cost time; this is consistent with LeDoux's remark that the importance of order scales inversely with the content signal of the data.

## Appendix J: Towards language models (explorations and one confirmation, LM1; not among the main results)

*All results in this appendix except the LM1 confirmation (fresh seeds 4000–4009, marked as such) are explorations on seeds 3800–3809 (and 3850–3851), with readings fixed before each run; they are not confirmations. The 60 000-step result and the r0-long and 10k checks were independently recomputed; the others were not.*

**Question.** Does steering by the training set (Result 1) survive when the task is trained the way a language model would see it? We changed one property at a time in a trainer that is bit-identical to the Section 2 setup when all switches are off (EXP-102; checked on 3 seeds, split F, at snapshots 50, 250, 1000 and 2000), with the engineered splits F and G of 10 seeds and 2000 full-batch steps.

**Format.** An explicit operator token (a + b =), a softmax over the whole vocabulary, and tied input/output embeddings each kept the steering clearly positive (pre-set reading 'holds'; paired differences to the reference between −0.76 and −0.05, CIs including 0): Δ_pow 7.41 [6.74, 8.17], 7.99 [7.52, 8.48] and 7.28 [6.38, 8.21] against 8.04 [7.59, 8.51] for the reference, 10/10 seeds each. With all three switches together and i.i.d. minibatches of 256 (EXP-112, 5000 steps), Δ_pow was 9.96 [9.44, 10.47] against 9.86 [9.43, 10.28] for the reference at the same batch size (paired +0.10 [−0.20, 0.40]).

**Next-token loss.** A language model also predicts the operands. With the loss on every position, the network must predict b after a, which it can only memorize for the training pairs. This delayed grokking by more than an order of magnitude (median 750 steps with the loss on all positions except b, 20/20 runs by 2000; 9 000–46 000 steps with it, 9/10 seeds by 60 000). After grokking Δ_pow was 4.40 [3.83, 4.91], below the reference in 9/9 seeds (paired −3.75 [−4.68, −2.97]), i.e. about 55 % of its value at step 2000; the pre-set reading was 'unclear' because the interval contains half the reference value. The comparison is at different step counts (22 000–47 000 against 2000). Training the reference longer did not close the gap in this exploration: its Δ_pow rose from 8.04 at step 2000 to 10.44 at 10 000 and 10.54 at 30 000, and at equal step counts the loss on all positions stayed below it in 10/10 seeds (−7.36 [−8.22, −6.31] at 10 000, −6.26 [−7.20, −5.15] at 30 000; exploration, independently recomputed). Equal step counts are not equal stages, however: with the loss on all positions only 1/20 runs had generalized by 10 000 and 13/20 by 30 000; in the 4 seeds in which both runs had generalized by 30 000 the gap was still negative in each (−2.6 to −6.8). Without the loss on the b position the steering held in full batch (8.26 [7.55, 8.96]), but under minibatches of 256 in the full language-model format it was smaller and grokking slower at 5000 steps (8.24 [6.78, 9.72]; paired −1.62 [−3.16, −0.13]; 13/20 runs generalized). At 10 000 steps 16/20 runs had generalized and the paired gap was −1.15 [−2.40, 0.08] (8/10 seeds negative), which by the pre-set rule reads as 'only delayed' (independently recomputed): no lasting weakening was shown, which is not the same as equality (the count lies exactly at the rule's threshold of 16/20, and the upper CI bound only just exceeds 0: 0.08, 0.06–0.14 across bootstrap seeds). Informally, a similar pattern (full-sequence loss favouring a memorized table over the algorithm) was reported for a composition task in the dihedral group D3 in a blog post (read via a summary tool only); we did not find a measurement of this delay or of its effect on data steering.

**Token frequencies.** In a language model, token counts could shape the number embeddings without any arithmetic. In the Section 2 model (answer loss, full batch), splits with exactly equal counts of every a, b and c = a + b (every number 34 times in every role; EXP-104, 2 seeds) still steered (Δ_pow > 1 in both seeds at all three levels of symmetry breaking, 6.0–10.1; not comparable in size with Result 1, because their mask target share is 0.65–0.74 against 0.17–0.19), so there the steering does not need a frequency signal. Nearly shift-invariant versions of these splits generalized in only 2 of 8 runs by 8000 steps, against 4/4 after stronger symmetry breaking, in line with the observation of Tomàs Bernal et al. (2026) for kernels that symmetric training sets can prevent generalization (2 seeds, descriptive; at the two lower levels 6 of 8 runs never generalized, so their Δ_pow describes non-generalized networks).

**A small language model (explorations).** A 13.9 M-parameter transformer trained from scratch on TinyStories with interleaved arithmetic sentences (tied embeddings; loss on the text and, inside the arithmetic sentences, on the answer tokens only, except where noted) learned the facts in both configurations with this answer-only loss (below); with 8.7 % arithmetic tokens and the loss on every position (EXP-105, 2 seeds, 10 000 steps) one seed began to learn them and the other did not, so arithmetic share and loss mode are confounded there (EXP-116, queued, tests the answer-only loss at 8.7 % with a longer 16 000-step budget); with about 79 % arithmetic tokens (EXP-114, 1 seed, P1-type splits) both runs of the F/G pair learned them between steps 1750 and 2000 and reached 0.98 and 0.99 accuracy on held-out facts by step 4000, and Δ_pow on the number-token rows was 5.60. With about 34 % arithmetic tokens and the same answer-only loss (EXP-113, answer arm, one F/G pair of the queued two-seed pilot), the model began to fit the facts only at step 9000 (after about 2.3 million fact presentations, against 1.2 million at 79 %), reached 0.98 and 0.95 held-out accuracy and Δ_pow 7.00 by step 16 000. In these four trained language models (seed 3862; exploration, EXP-118), removing the Fourier subspace of the run's own five targets from the number-token rows lowered held-out fact accuracy from 0.95–0.99 to 0.03–0.30, while removing the other split's targets or any of four control sets left it at 0.93–0.99; with tied embeddings this ablation acts on input and output vectors alike. **Confirmation of use (LM1-F, frozen before any ablation; independently recomputed, identical to within 2.2·10⁻⁸).** In the ten LM1 models, removing the Fourier subspace of the run's own five target frequencies from the number-token rows lowered held-out fact accuracy far more than removing the other split's targets (mean C̄ 0.882 [0.836, 0.918], above the registered minimum effect of 0.1; one-sided sign-permutation p = 1/1024, the resolution limit; 10 of 10 seeds with C̄ > 0): median held-out accuracy 0.982 at baseline, 0.048 without the own targets, 0.979 without the other split's targets and 0.978 without a single control set (median over the four control sets). With tied embeddings this ablation acts on input and output vectors alike, so it shows that the steered frequencies are used by the model, not whether the input or the output side uses them. **Confirmation (LM1, frozen before any run, 10 fresh seeds; independently recomputed).** In the same 14 M-parameter language model (about 79 % arithmetic tokens, loss on the text and on the answer tokens, tied embeddings, 6000 steps), the engineered fact splits steered the number-token embedding on 10 fresh seeds: mean Δ_pow 5.32 [4.86, 5.73] at step 6000 (range 3.96–6.40), 10/10 seeds above the registered minimum effect 1 (exact sign-permutation p = 1/1024, the smallest attainable with 10 seeds, assuming symmetry about 1 under H0); held-out fact accuracy was ≥ 0.5 in 20/20 runs (0.898–0.995). This is one configuration with a high arithmetic share and an energy measure on tied embeddings; it does not show steering at a few percent arithmetic data or functional use, and these P1-type splits also carry the targets in the number counts (see the equal-count splits below). Secondary and descriptive: in 9 of 10 pairs the first snapshot with Δ_pow > 1 came before the first with training-fact accuracy ≥ 0.1 in both arms (8 by one snapshot of 250 steps, 1 by two), in 1 of 10 at the same snapshot (it did not precede the fit onset in 1 of 10). In both the language model and the Section 2 model, the steering became visible within one or two snapshots of the fit to the training pairs: in the Section 2 model (EXP-103, 50 seeds, post hoc) the first snapshot with Δ_pow > 1 and the first with training accuracy ≥ 0.1 in both arms had the same median (step 75); in the language model this onset came only after thousands of steps. In the Section 2 model this coincidence also held across a fourfold change of the learning rate at constant lr·wd (EXP-103, 10 paired seeds, post hoc: median fit onsets 29 to 92 steps, steering onsets later by a median factor of 1.10–1.17 in each setting), which by itself does not separate a dependence of the steering on the fit from a shared clock. *Supplementary figure* (`figures/fig14_lm_onset.py`, EXP-114, one F/G pair, exploration): Δ_pow on the number-token rows stays below 0.2 until step 1500, reaches 0.70 at 1750 and 3.62 at 2000, when the training-fact accuracy first exceeds 0.1 in both runs (0.80/0.70), and grows to 5.60 by step 4000; held-out fact accuracy follows the training facts with a short delay (0.98/0.99 at 4000). With tied embeddings the number rows also serve as output vectors, and in P1-type splits the counts of each number carry target structure, so a positive Δ_pow in a language model need not come from the pair structure alone; with exactly equal counts of every number in every role (EXP-104 splits, EXP-115, 2 seeds, exploration) the steering reached Δ_pow 5.23 and 1.83 at step 2500 and fell back to 4.35 and 0.96 by step 4000, so with equal counts one of two seeds kept Δ_pow well above 1 and the other ended just below it (pre-set reading 'unclear'; the F run of the second seed did not generalize, held-out accuracy 0.63). Post hoc (2 seeds), the fall is not a dilution: Δ_pow compares own-target with other-arm-target energy, so energy on other frequencies cannot lower it. Own-target energy still grew, but the energy on the other arm's targets grew faster in all four runs, most strongly in one run per seed, which carries most of the fall (×3.10 against ×1.39 and ×6.41 against ×3.13 between steps 2500 and 4000; also faster than the remaining frequencies, ×1.89 and ×2.78), whereas with P1-type splits the other arm's targets lost energy (×0.93 and ×0.89; EXP-114, 1 seed). The same flat splits in the toy model show no fall by the end of the common window (1 525 and 100 steps after both arms had generalized; exploration). With untied input and output embeddings (EXP-117, exploration, 2 seeds, P1-type splits, 6000 steps) the input rows of the number tokens were steered (Δ_in 6.44 and 5.54; held-out facts 0.92–0.97), so the effect is not only a property of shared output vectors; Δ_out of the output rows was also positive (4.04 and 4.74; descriptive). In these untied models, removing the run's own target subspace from the input rows alone lowered held-out accuracy as much as removing it from both sides (0.02–0.07 against 0.01–0.09), removing it from the output rows alone lowered it by 26–55 points, and removing the other split's targets left it at 0.92–0.97 on every side (single control sets 0.85–0.97; EXP-120, exploration on the same 4 models; pre-set reading "unclear" because one output-side contrast, 0.27, fell below the preset 0.3). Descriptively, not as a pre-set reading, the steered frequencies matter mainly on the input side and partly on the output side (the two projections are different interventions, so their sizes are not strictly comparable). With the same trainer and tied embeddings (EXP-119, exploration, 2 seeds, 6000 steps), held-out facts from engineered splits reached accuracy 0.5 within 17–78 steps of the training facts, while a uniform random split of the same size was memorized equally early (training facts at 1870 and 2112 steps against 1872–2343) but did not reach 0.5 on held-out facts within 6000 steps (held-out accuracy stayed at about 0.3 from the end of memorization to step 6000, 0.33 and 0.32 at the end; pre-set reading "constructed faster", ratio q ≥ 3.15 and ≥ 2.61, censored). Descriptively (not pre-set; 2 seeds), the difference in the language model lies after memorization (training accuracy ≥ 0.5 was reached equally early), not in an earlier onset of learning; whether the random split would generalize later is not known. Post hoc (reading fixed before computing), the plateau consists of the held-out facts whose mirrored pair (b, a) was trained (0.99 and 1.00 correct, against 0.03 on the others; chance 0.009), whereas the engineered-split models answer both groups (0.97–1.00; 0.968 in one run): by step 6000 the model with the random split behaved as if it had learned the swap a + b = b + a (it answered correctly almost exactly where the mirrored fact was trained) and hardly any addition beyond it. That the composition rather than the amount of training facts sets the pace of grokking is known for implicit reasoning (Wang et al. 2024); here size and repetition are equal and only the choice of pairs differs, but that choice also puts the targets into the number counts, so a count effect is not excluded. A random split with exactly flat counts (EXP-121, exploration, 2 runs with the model seeds of the equal-count block above; every number 34 times in each role; its difference set was drawn at random, so no frequencies were chosen, but the construction still concentrates the mask spectrum on a few random frequencies: top-5 mask share 0.16, against 0.27–0.30 in the equal-count F/G splits, 0.17–0.19 in the engineered splits of EXP-119 and 0.105–0.107 in its random split) did not stall within 4000 steps: held-out facts reached 0.5 570 and 223 steps after the training facts (pre-set reading "unclear" against the preset bounds of 300 and 1000; the equal-count engineered splits of the same seeds, on a larger test set: 25–300), and post hoc (reading fixed before computing) the models also answered held-out facts without a trained mirror (0.68 and 0.98). Descriptively, in these two runs a choice of target frequencies was not needed to avoid the commutativity plateau. Uneven counts alone do not explain the plateau of the ordinary random split either, since the engineered splits of EXP-119 have equally uneven counts (coefficient of variation of the counts of a and b 0.13–0.16, random split 0.14–0.15) and generalized quickly; post hoc and across three blocks with different seeds and test sets, the splits that did not stay on the plateau all had a concentrated mask spectrum (by the largest single-frequency mask power, not the top-5 share: at least 1.6 times that of the two random splits; the cut was read off after the fact, and both plateau splits come from one block), which is consistent with the first-order picture that a spectral peak of the mask, wherever it lies, would be needed, but this was not tested directly.

**A commutativity stage before grokking (explorations with pre-set readings; pilot EXP-122 on 4 + 4 runs, main block EXP-123).** The language-model plateau above made us split held-out accuracy in the Section 2 transformer by whether the mirrored pair (b, a) of a held-out pair (a, b) was trained (about 30 % of held-out pairs in every split; this model has position embeddings, so commutativity is not built in). On the random splits of the 20 R5 units (same initializations and test sets as Section 4, whose generalization times were known; readings, code and thresholds fixed before the runs; disclosures in the EXP-123 record), held-out pairs with a trained mirror reached accuracy 0.5 at least 100 steps before the other held-out pairs (or while these stayed below 0.5 up to 8000 steps, 1 unit) in 18 of 18 units where this was determinable (one-sided sign test, Holm-p 8·10⁻⁶; the same 18 of 18 at thresholds 0.3 and 0.7, post hoc; in the two remaining units the mirrored pairs never reached 0.5, and neither unit generalized within 8000 steps). So on random splits the test accuracy is first carried by held-out pairs whose mirror was trained, consistent with a learned symmetry a + b = b + a (median 4150 steps to 0.5 on mirrored pairs over the 18 units that reached it), and the other pairs follow in a late, steep jump (median 5325 steps over the 17 units that reached 0.5; Figure 15). He et al. (2026a) report the corresponding split of test accuracy at the end of memorization in a two-layer network whose input h_a + h_b makes it commutative by construction; here the symmetry has to be learned. The pre-set hypothesis that engineered splits mainly shorten the second stage was not supported: when the mirrored pairs first reached 0.5, the other pairs were further on engineered than on random splits by a mean of only 0.041 [0.020, 0.062], below the pre-set minimum effect of 0.05 (14 of 18 units; sign-permutation p = 0.001), and post hoc, in absolute steps, engineered splits shortened the commutativity stage more (geometric mean ×11.1 over 17 units) than the remaining stage (×4.6). The count-matched control D behaved like the random split in this measure (difference in the other pairs' accuracy at the mirrored pairs' 0.5 crossing 0.003, 11 of 17 units, p = 0.40), although fewer D units generalized (14 of 20 against 16 of 20). So in the toy model the engineered splits act mostly on the first stage, whereas the random-split language models stalled in the second; the two settings need not share a mechanism. All units come from the R5 block, so this is not an independent confirmation.

*Figure 15* (`figures/fig15_commutativity_stages.py`, EXP-123, 20 R5 units per arm, exploration): held-out accuracy on pairs whose mirrored pair was trained (solid) and on the others (dashed) against training step divided by the run's generalization step; thin lines are units, thick lines medians over the units that generalized (16/20 random, 14/20 count-matched control D, 20/20 engineered E2); units that did not generalize are drawn against 8000 steps. On random splits the mirrored pairs rise from early on and the others jump late (their median crosses 0.5 near 0.9 of the generalization step); on engineered splits both medians reach 0.5 earlier in relative time (about 0.4 and 0.75 against 0.7 and 0.9), and the others rise gradually instead of jumping (a change of shape, not of duration).

**Context.** Pretrained language models compute addition with Fourier features of the number tokens (Zhou, Fu, Sharan and Jia 2024) or a helix (Kantamneni and Tegmark 2025) and carry circular features for periodic concepts such as weekdays and months (Engels et al. 2024); models trained from scratch on addition use mainly low frequencies (Zhou, Fu, Sharan and Jia 2024), and data, tokenizer and architecture shape which periods appear (Fu et al. 2026). These works describe which number features models end up with; the explorations in this appendix ask whether the choice of arithmetic facts prescribes them. In our searches (2026-09-28 and 2026-09-29) we did not find this question addressed for a model trained from scratch; this is provisional.

## Appendix K: Additional details for the main text (passages shortened in Sections 1-7, verbatim)

**For Section 1:** Because all of these results use full-batch training, while LeDoux's order effect arises under minibatch training, Section 6 (L0) tests whether the steering survives minibatch training and what happens when a structured example order favours a different frequency than the set. All claims hold for one model family and for constructed splits. The random-split, speed-up and persistence results (R4, R5, Section 5) hold for addition mod 113 only, except the persistence window in embedding energy, which R11 also confirmed for addition mod 97 and multiplication mod 113. Explorations, resets, the optimizer clock of the lock-in, and a first-order account are in the appendix.

**For Section 2:** In the isotropic-Jacobian model at initialization, B's expected first-order gradient at A's targets points partly against A's (about −0.38 of A's own push). This is an expectation, not a measured gradient, and how the term acts after 25–50 steps was not measured.

**For Section 2:** A committed manifest stores code hashes; a wrapper checks them before, during and after training and binds every output to the manifest, and the analysis accepts only bound runs. In most blocks one frozen job was first run as a smoke test and counted as a regular run.

**For Section 3:** *Post hoc (exploration on the same units, independently recomputed):* a network's strongest (highest-energy) frequencies rank high in its own split's coherent mask spectrum M0c: its five strongest frequencies sit on average at the 78th percentile of the own split's M0c against about the 50th for the other split of the unit (difference 0.28 [0.26, 0.30] at step 2000, 60/60 units; 0.25 at step 8000; 0.29 already at step 250) and absent at initialization. Because the splits are assigned at random and independently of the initialization, this difference is an effect of the split; that it acts through the mask spectrum is consistent with the first-order account (Appendix G) but not isolated here. Ranked before training, the split's mask spectrum also predicts the five strongest frequencies better than the embedding energy at initialization: overlap with the learned top five 0.34 against 0.19 (chance 0.09; difference 0.14 [0.11, 0.18] over units; a placebo with another unit's split gives 0.10). This predictor ignores the phase alignment that decides the winner per neuron in He et al. (2026a), who moreover train on 75 % of the pairs (here 30 %), so it does not test their mechanism.

**For Section 3:** LeDoux (2026) reports the same frequency across random training subsets under a structured example order at p = 9973. Plausibly that is a different regime (not measured), dominated by the order signal and with ≈ 80× more pairs (Section 6 probes 240 steps per epoch: order effects only on random splits, pilot). The spectral fluctuations of a uniform random subset shrink roughly as 1/√n, so there they are about 9× smaller.

**For Section 4:** All censoring is administrative at the common bound of 8000 steps, so the mean bounded time is the restricted mean survival time; post hoc, its ratios are 5.8 [4.6, 7.6] (R against ε = 2, targets A) and 6.9 [6.0, 8.1] (D against ε = 2), consistent with the registered geometric-mean ratios.

**For Section 5:** Zeroing Adam's first moment at the switch lowered π from 0.340 (control arm of the separate block N28) to 0.189, and ten extra pre-switch steps with the same reset compensated this (N28; non-inferiority, margin 0.05). This is compatible with an "exposure" reading, not a proof of it. That the first moment carries such a signal is known from other settings (Sweeney 2026; Xu 2026). Post hoc, a scalar Adam model puts it at 6.5–10.8 update-equivalents at t = 25–35 (Appendix C).

**For Section 5:** All 60 destination-only runs generalized by step 2000; of the switch runs, between 16/30 and 26/30 did at t = 10–30 (20/30 and 22/30 at t = 25, both directions; 17/30 and 16/30 at t = 20), and at least 28/30 at t ≥ 40. The others count at the bound, so C(t) underestimates the delay where it is largest.

**For Section 6:** A first-order computation from the split files, made before any run (Appendix I), predicted that at 30 % data the order can compete with the set within the lock-in window only for long epochs: not at batch 256 (15 steps per epoch), at the edge at batch 64, and clearly at batch 16 (240 steps per epoch), which was therefore added before any run; at batch 16 the default weight decay 1 did not generalize in 30 000 steps, so this arm uses weight decay 0.1 (a regime change). This computation assumed the full-batch lock-in window and is only a necessary condition; the window under minibatches turned out to be later (below).

**For Section 6:** A drift reading based on the sign-like updates of Adam (Li et al., 2024; derived in this project, AI-assisted, see the AI use disclosure) predicts t½ ∝ 1/(lr·√B); the measured slope lies in the registered square-root band but slightly above 0.5, and the model does not predict the weaker learning-rate effect at small batches.

**For Section 7:** Minibatch training and data order are tested only in L0 (Section 6); there, steering under i.i.d. minibatches of 256 and 64 was confirmed on 10 fresh seeds (energy measure, at the end of the budget) and held at batch 16 with weight decay 0.1 in a pilot; a conflict between set and a fixed order was not testable at 30 % data under the pre-set rule, and the order shifted the spectrum only on random splits at batch 16 (pilot); under i.i.d. minibatches the lock-in half-point grew with batch size, to 58, 114 and 289 steps at batch 1024, 256 and 64 (N54b, 10 fresh seeds, energy measure; about √(N/B) at the default learning rate), so the 25–50-step figure of Result 3 is a full-batch result.

**For Figure caption:** Across the P1 arms, the mask share partly predicts which target lags (post hoc, seen seeds: mean within-arm Spearman 0.32 for addition mod 113, initial W_E power 0.125; `P1_posthoc_within.json`).

**For Section 5:** 19/20 seeds generalized; restricted to them, the contrasts are 0.898 and 0.591.

**For Section 5:** The cost of the other-target switch here (+0.66 [0.48, 0.83]) and C(25) in R6 (+0.85 [0.73, 0.96]) are separate estimates on different fresh seeds and splits; their intervals overlap.

**For Section 6:** In this pilot the order thus shifted the spectrum on random splits but not on engineered splits, where it only cost time, consistent with LeDoux's remark that the importance of order scales inversely with the content signal of the data. SGD with momentum could not be calibrated and is not evaluable.

**For Section 7:** Under minibatches, doubling the learning rate shortened lock-in to ×0.58 at batch 1024 but only to ×0.85 at batch 64 (N54b), so no single summed-learning-rate clock holds there.

**For Section 7:** (v) *Horizon:* switch experiments are read at most 2000–4000 steps after the switch (R6/R8: until step 2000 in total; the minibatch series EXP-107/108 and N54b at step 5000, up to ≈ 4980 steps after the switch). Other final models are read at 2000–12 000 steps. Much longer training is untested.

**Superseded caption of an earlier Figure 4 (pilot version; the current Figure 4 is above):** **L0: training-set composition against data order under minibatch training.** Pilot EXP-100 (8 seeds, exploration); the L0 confirmation on 10 fresh seeds is reported in the text. Drawn by `fig11_l0_set_vs_order.py` from the analysis output; the title line gives the pre-fixed pilot readings. Left: Δ_pow at the end of each arm's budget (not at equal steps), dots per seed, mean with 95 % bootstrap CI per arm (full batch 2000 and 30 000 steps, i.i.d. minibatch 256 and 64, SGD with momentum marked 'not evaluable' because its learning rate could not be calibrated, fixed stride order). Right: share of the embedding energy on the stride-order frequencies O = {11, 12, 22, 23, 34, 45} (chance 6/56), i.i.d. against stride order at batch 256, for the engineered splits (F and G averaged) and the random split. The conditional stride arm at batch 64 is reported in the text, not drawn.

**For Section 1:** In recursive feature machines, training sets that are invariant under a subgroup of the task's symmetry group (for example, with the fixed points of a reflection removed) prevent generalization, and the learned feature matrix then encodes only that subgroup; breaking the symmetry of the training set restores generalization (Tomàs Bernal et al. 2026; kernels only, symmetric splits, no prescribed frequencies).

**For Section 1:** one after 50 steps does not (it even reaches the threshold earlier than training on the destination split alone), and

**For Section 3:** In the other three tasks the steering is not a pre-grokking transient: in separate stored runs (P2d/P2e, 20 other seeds per task, median generalization at step 725, 1225 for addition mod 97; post hoc exploration, not P1) Δ_pow stayed positive in every seed at every stored step and grew after generalization before levelling off without falling back, e.g. 7.77 at step 2000 and 9.44 [8.99, 9.90] at step 4000 for addition mod 113.

**For Section 3:** Post hoc, the five strongest frequencies of a network rank higher in its own split's coherent mask spectrum (M0c) than in the other split's, already at step 250 and not at initialization (exploration).

**For Section 4:** Post hoc, a higher early target share goes with earlier generalization; whether the speed-up runs entirely through this early signal is open.

**For Section 5:** All 60 destination-only runs generalized by step 2000; switch runs that had not (4–14 of 30 per direction at t = 10–30, at most 2 at t ≥ 40) count at the bound, so C(t) underestimates the delay where it is largest.

**For Section 5:** **The window generalizes beyond addition mod 113 (R11, the same 30 fresh seeds for both tasks, independently recomputed).** With the EXP-044 protocol (switch F → G at 25 or 50 steps, one direction, then 2000 steps; π from final embedding energy), the first split's choice persisted mostly after 50 but not after 25 steps also in addition mod 97 (π(25) = 0.38, π(50) = 0.90; difference +0.52 [0.45, 0.59], 30/30 seeds) and in multiplication mod 113, which in discrete-log coordinates is addition in Z₁₁₂ plus a zero token (0.27 and 0.74; +0.47 [0.40, 0.54], 30/30). All six registered tests held (Holm); the weakest was that the second split wins at 25 steps in addition mod 97 (0.5 − π(25) = +0.12 [0.07, 0.18], 23/30). This is the embedding-energy measure only; the ablation contrast and the time cost were not re-tested there.

**For Section 6:** **Design.** Addition mod 113, the setup of Section 2, AdamW with i.i.d. minibatches of 256 or 64 pairs; a pilot (EXP-100, 8 seeds) also ran full batch with a matched 30 000-step budget and SGD with momentum. The conflict arm uses a fixed stride order after LeDoux, pairs sorted by (a mod 10, a) and identical in every epoch, which puts its spectral weight on the frequencies O = {11, 12, 22, 23, 34, 45}; the targets of the engineered splits exclude O. A first-order computation made before any run (Appendix I) predicted that at 30 % data the order can compete with the set within the full-batch lock-in window only for long epochs (a necessary condition only; the minibatch window turned out later, below), so an arm with batch 16 (240 steps per epoch) was added before any run; it uses weight decay 0.1, because weight decay 1 did not generalize there in 30 000 steps (a regime change). LeDoux's order effect was strong at 0.3 % data (≈ 1165 steps per epoch); our regime is far from it. Readings were fixed before the runs; the conflict is judged only if the order is shown to act at all.

**For Section 6:** At batch 256 and 64 the stride order did not shift the learned frequencies (peak frequency in O in 0/16 runs each; order-share difference on the engineered splits +0.004 [−0.003, 0.015] and +0.005 [−0.000, 0.011]), so by the pre-set rule the conflict was not testable there. At batch 16 the conflict was again not testable by the pre-set rule (order-alone reading 'unclear'). Descriptively, the order raised the order share on random splits (+0.16 [0.07, 0.24]; about 0 in the three seeds whose i.i.d. run already carried 0.20–0.24 on O) but not on the engineered splits, where it only delayed generalization (0.67 log2 [0.42, 0.93], ≈ ×1.6, 15/16 pairs).

**For Section 6:** Under i.i.d. minibatches of 256, a switch after 25 or 50 steps left no persistent trace (pilot, 8 seeds: π ≈ 0, against π(50) = 0.87 in full batch on the same seeds). The window lies later in steps and earlier in epochs (pilots EXP-107/108): the half-point is near 133 steps (8.9 epochs) at batch 256, against about 31 steps (31 epochs) in full batch (linear interpolation, energy measure).

**For Section 7:** Minibatch training and data order are tested only in L0 (Section 6): steering survived i.i.d. minibatches of 256 and 64 (energy measure, at the end of the budget), a conflict between set and a fixed order was not testable at 30 % data under the pre-set rule, and the lock-in took more steps at smaller batches (N54b, energy measure), so the 25–50-step figure of Result 3 is a full-batch result.

**For Section 7:** The persistence does not follow the step count alone (a descriptive reading of R3; its Λ clock was not confirmed). With Adam's moment windows rescaled to summed learning rate, it matched summed learning rate in one confirmed equivalence cell (lr × 0.25) and was consistent with it in a second (lr × 2, direction confirmed, equality descriptive; R9, addition mod 113, π measure; Appendix).
